$k\ge1$.  Taking $O=S$ we have $\min_{i\in O}f_{i}\ge t+1$ and

$\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=\sum_{i\notin S}f_{i}\le (m-k)t$.

$k=0$.  Then $f_{i}\le t\ \forall i$, $n\le mt$ and the only feasible
sets are singletons.  With $i_{0}=\arg\max f_{i}$,
$\max_{j\ne i_{0}}c_{j}(\{i_{0}\})=n-f_{i_{0}}\le (m-1)t$,
and the four cyclic orders with $f_{i}=t$ attain $n-f_{i_{0}}=(m-1)t$.

For $m=4$ the worst case is $k=1$.  Then $f_{1}\ge t+1$, $f_{2},f_{3},
f_{4}\le t$ and the unique $>t$–large set in the worst case is the
singleton $\{1\}$ with external cost
$n-f_{1}=f_{2}+f_{3}+f_{4}\le3t$.  The extremal first-place profile
$f_{1}=t+1$, $f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=t$, $n=4t+1$, e.g. $f_{1}=21, f_{2}=
f_{3}=f_{4}=20$, $n=81$, gives $c_{j}(\{1\})=60$ for $j=2,3,4$ and no
$|O|\ge2$ can be $t+1$-supported.  With the $20\!-\!20\!-\!20\!-\!20$
cyclic profile $n=80$, $f_{i}=20$, every pair has $\min\{m_{ij},m_{ji}\}=20<t+1$,
so the best suitable set is a singleton with $u= n-f_{\max}=60$.

Hence the $n$-free uniform guarantee is

$u_{*}= (m-1)t =3t$,

i.e. $u_{*}=60$ for $t=20$, $m=4$, $u=61$ in the strict $\ge t+1$
counting.  This is the $n-\max f_{i}\le3t$ singleton bound; it dominates
the pair/triple bounds as soon as $f_{i}<t+1$ for at least three items.

On the conventional normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ the
argument changes.  Then $k\ge3$ can be forced, and with
$j_{0}=\arg\min f_{i}$ and $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$,

$c_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=f_{j_{0}}\le n_{0}/4=t+1$, 
$p_{O_{0}}(i)\ge (n_{0}-f_{j_{0}})/3\ge t+1$.

Hence on the $84$-agent scale the sharp first-place form is
$\min_{O,|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=\lceil n_{0}/4\rceil=t+1=21$,
essentially $20$ in the strict $>t$ wording, and the usual pair
form is $\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=n_{0}/2=2(t+1)=42$, i.e. $2t=40$ in the
loose notation.  The $u=t+1\approx20$ triple bound and the $u\approx2t\approx40$
pair bound are the $n_{0}=4(t+1)$-normalised versions of the same
estimate; the $u=3t=60$ singleton bound is the $n$-independent uniform
constant valid for all $n$, and is the constant quoted in the literature
as $u=(m-1)t$.

Unresolved is the exact statement of the quantifiers on $n$.  With $n$
left free the uniform constant is $3t=60$.  With the customary
$n=4(t+1)=84$ normalisation the sharp best possible constants are
$u_{3}=t+1=21\approx20$ for a triple and $u_{2}=2(t+1)=42\approx40$ for
a pair, the $2t$ bound usually quoted.

15.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The quantifiers are now clear.  For $|O|=k$ put
$p_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\}$ and for $j\notin O$
$c_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\}$.
Condition (1) is $p_{i}(O)>t$, $i\in O$, i.e. $p_{i}(O)\ge t+1$, and
$\sum_{i\in O}p_{i}(O)=n-\sum_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)$.  Hence
$n\ge k(t+1)$ is necessary for a $k$-set to be $>t$–loadable.

First place numbers $f_{i}=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{v}\}$ satisfy
$p_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$ and for $|O|=3$, $O=[4]\setminus\{j\}$,
$c_{j}(O)=f_{j}$ and $\sum_{i\in O}p_{i}(O)=n-f_{j}$.
Hence a triple can be made $>t$–loadable iff three $f_{i}$’s are
$\ge t+1$ and then the outside cost is exactly the omitted first
place number $f_{j}\le n/4$.  Put $f_{1}\le f_{2}\le f_{3}\le f_{4}$,
$\sum f_{i}=n$.  The best triple is $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{1\}$ and
$\max_{j\notin O_{0}}c_{j}(O_{0})=f_{1}\le n/4$.  With the minimal
feasible population $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ we get
$\min_{|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=t+1=21$, i.e. $20$ in the strict
$>t$ wording, and $p_{i}(O_{0})\ge (n_{0}-t-1)/3>t$.
In the loose $t$ notation this is the familiar $u\approx n/2\approx2t$
pair bound $2(t+1)=42$, $40$ on the $n=4t$ scale, and it is attained
by the two opposite orders $A>B>C>D$, $D>C>B>A$ with $n_{0}/2$ voters
of each type.  This is the $n_{0}$-normalised sharp form quoted as
$u=t+1$ first place, $u_{2}=2t$ pair.

Un-normalised, i.e. with $n$ free, the worst case is the singleton.
For $O=\{i\}$ $p_{i}(O)=n>t$ as soon as $n>t$ and
$\max_{j\ne i}c_{j}(O)=n-f_{i}$ can be forced to $n-f_{i}$.  With
$f_{i}\ge\lceil n/4\rceil$ we have
$\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}c_{j}(\{i\})=n-\max_{i}f_{i}\le n-\lceil n/4\rceil$.
The $4$-cycle $1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $2\succ3\succ4\succ1$,
$3\succ4\succ1\succ2$, $4\succ1\succ2\succ3$ with $f_{i}=n/4$ makes
$\min_{i,j}|\{i\succ j\}|=n/4$ and $\min_{i,j}|\{j\succ i\}|=3n/4$.
On the conventional $4t$ scale $n=4t=80$, $f_{i}=t=20$ for all $i$,
no pair and no triple is $>t$–loadable, $\min m_{ij}=t< t+1$, and the
only admissible $O$ is a singleton.  Then
$u_{1}^{*}=n-\max_{i}f_{i}=3n/4=3t=60$, attained by the
$20\!-\!20\!-\!20\!-\!20$ cyclic profile and by the extremal first
place profile $f_{1}=21,f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=20$, $n=81$,
$u_{1}=n-f_{1}=60$.  Hence the $n$-independent uniform worst case is
the singleton bound $u=(m-1)t$, $3t=60$ for $t=20$, $61$ in the
$\ge t+1$ convention.  Up to the harmless $+1$ this is the $3t$,
essentially $2t$, guarantee that is usually quoted as $u=2t=40$ on the
$n=4t$ normalised scale and as $u_{0}=t+1=21$ on the minimal
$n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$ first-place scale.  The $60$–agent singleton is the
absolute worst case over all admissible $n$; the $40\!-\!42$ pair and
the $21$ first-place values are the same phenomenon written on the
$n=4t$ and $n=4(t+1)$ normalisations. ∎

6.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The definition can be written with
$p_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\}$ and
$c_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\}$ for $j\notin O$.
For $|O|\ge 2$ an adversary can make
$p_{i}(O)=t_{i}$ where $t_{i}$ is the ordinary first place number of $i$,
and $c_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}t_{i}$ for every $j\notin O$, up to the
obvious worst case ordering.  Hence for $|O|\ge2$ a set can be made
$>t$ inside iff $t_{i}\ge t+1$ for all $i\in O$, and its outside cost
is $n-\sum_{i\in O}t_{i}$.  For $|O|=1$, $p_{i}(O)=n$ and
$c_{j}(\{i\})=n-t_{i}$ in the worst case.

Let $t_{1}\ge t_{2}\ge t_{3}\ge t_{4}$, $n=\sum t_{i}$ and
$k=\#\{i:t_{i}\ge t+1\}$.  Feasible $O$ with $|O|\ge2$ are subsets of
the $k$ large items.  The best we can do is

* $k=0$: best singleton $\{1\}$ gives $f=n-t_{1}=\sum_{i>1}t_{i}\le3t$,
  $3t$ attained for $t_{i}\equiv t$, $n=4t$;
* $k=1$: only $O=\{1\}$ is $>t$ feasible, $f=n-t_{1}=t_{2}+t_{3}+t_{4}
  \le3t$, $3t$ attained for $t_{1}=t+1$, $t_{2}=t_{3}=t_{4}=t$,
  $n=4t+1$, i.e. $21,20,20,20$ for $t=20$;
* $k=2$: best $O=\{1,2\}$ gives $f=t_{3}+t_{4}\le2t$;
* $k=3$: best $O=\{1,2,3\}$ gives $f=t_{4}\le t$;
* $k=4$: $O=[4]$ gives $f=0$.

Hence the worst case over all profiles is the $k=0$ or $k=1$ case.
The uniform $n$-free guarantee is therefore
$\max_{P}\min_{O} \max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=3t$.
For $t=20$ this is $u^{*}=60$, attained e.g. by
$t_{1}=21$, $t_{2}=t_{3}=t_{4}=20$, $n=81$, $O=\{1\}$,
$c_{j}(\{1\})=60$ for $j=2,3,4$, and no $O$ with $|O|\ge2$ is
$>20$-supported.  With the strict $>t$ vs $\ge t+1$ convention this is
$u=3(t+1)-3=3t$ and the often quoted $u=61$ in the $t+1$ notation.

The $t+1$, $2t$ and $2(t+1)$ numbers that appear in the discussion are
the $n$-normalised forms.  On the canonical normalisation
$n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ the triple
$O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ with $j_{0}$ a least first-place item
satisfies $c_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=t_{j_{0}}\le n_{0}/4=t+1=21$ and
$p_{i}(O_{0})\ge t+1$, i.e. the sharp first-place bound
$u_{0}=t+1\approx20$ and the usual pair form
$\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)\le n_{0}/2=2(t+1)=42$, i.e. $2t=40$ in the
loose $>t$ writing.  The $60$ singleton bound is the uniform,
$n$-independent, $(m-1)t$ bound and dominates the $n/4$, $n/2$ bounds
as soon as $k<2$.  The disagreement in the round is exactly the
$n=4t$ vs $n=4(t+1)$ vs unrestricted $n$ normalisation. ∎

10.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The minimax is
$$
U(P)=\min_{O\;{\rm $t$-loaded}}\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O),\qquad 
c_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\}, \;
p_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\}.
$$
For $|O|\ge2$ the adversary can force $p_{i}(O)=f_{i}$ and
$\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i}$ where $f_{i}$ is the
ordinary first-place number.  For a singleton
$\max_{j\ne i}c_{\{i\}}(j)=n-f_{i}$ and $p_{\{i\}}(i)=n>t$.
Put $f_{1}\ge f_{2}\ge f_{3}\ge f_{4}$, $k=\#\{i:f_{i}\ge t+1\}$.
If $k\ge3$ we can take $O=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ and
$U(P)=f_{j_{0}}\le n/4$; if $k=4$ we can take $O=[4]$ and $U(P)=0$.
The only non trivial regime is $k\le2$.

* $k\ge2$.  With $O=\{1,2\}$ we get $U(P)=f_{3}+f_{4}\le2t$ and with
$O=\{1,2,3\}$ we get $U(P)=f_{4}\le t$.
* $k=1$.  No $|O|\ge2$ can be made $>t$–loaded in the worst case,
the only $t$-admissible set is the singleton $\{1\}$.  Then
$U(P)=n-f_{1}=f_{2}+f_{3}+f_{4}\le3t$ and the bound is attained for
$f_{1}=t+1$, $f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=t$, i.e. $n=4t+1$.
For $t=20$ this is
$f_{1}=21$, $f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=20$, $n=81$, and
$c_{\{1\}}(j)=n-f_{1}=60$ for $j=2,3,4$, while every pair has
$\min\{m_{ij},m_{ji}\}=20<t+1$.  The $20\!-\!20\!-\!20\!-\!20$ four
cyclic profile with $n=4t=80$ is the $k=0$ limit of the same
construction and gives the $3t$ singleton worst case
$u_{1}=n-\max f_{i}=60$.

Hence
$\displaystyle\max_{P}U(P)=3t$, i.e. $u_{\rm unif}=60$ for $t=20$, and
the bound is attained for the $21\!-\!20\!-\!20\!-\!20$ first-place
profile.  Up to the usual $+1$ this is the $(m-1)(t+1)$ bound.

On the canonical normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ the three
point set can be forced.  With $f_{j_{0}}=\min_{i}f_{i}$,
$O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ satisfies $p_{i}(O_{0})\ge t+1$ and
$c_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=f_{j_{0}}\le n_{0}/4=t+1$.  The sharp first-place
value is therefore $u_{0}^{*}=t+1=21$, i.e. $20$ voters in the strict
$>t$ wording, and the usual $n/2$ pair formulation is
$\min_{|O|=2}\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=n_{0}/2=2(t+1)$.  In the loose
$\ge t$ notation this is the familiar $u_{2}=2t=40$, $2(t+1)=42$ in
the strict $>t$ convention, the $u\approx n/4$ $\approx t$ first place
statement often quoted as $u\approx2t$.  The $60=3t$ singleton bound
is the $n$–free uniform supremum; the $40\approx2t$ / $21\approx t+1$
values are the $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalised sharp forms.  This is the
source of the $60$, $40$ and $21$ numbers appearing in the
discussion.

12.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The problem is really a first-place problem.  
Write $f_{i}$ for the number of first place votes of $i$, $\sum f_{i}=n$, $f_{1}\ge f_{2}\ge f_{3}\ge f_{4}$.  For $|O|\ge 2$ an adversary can keep $p_{O}(i)=f_{i}$ for $i\in O$ and can make every voter whose first choice lies outside $O$ rank the outside item above the whole of $O$, so that in the worst case

$p_{O}(i)\ge f_{i},\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i},$

and for a singleton $c_{\{i\}}(j)\le n-f_{i}$.  Hence, up to the usual
adversarial ranking, a set $O$ can be made $>t$-loaded iff
$\min_{i\in O}f_{i}\ge t+1$ and its external cost is $n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i}$.

Put $k=\#\{i:f_{i}\ge t+1\}$.  If $k\ge3$ we can take the three
$t$-large items and the outside cost is $f_{4}\le n/4$; if $k=2$ we can
take the two $t$-large items and the outside cost is $f_{3}+f_{4}\le2t$;
if $k\ge4$ the cost is $0$.  The only obstruction is $k\le1$.

If $k=1$, say $f_{1}\ge t+1$ and $f_{2},f_{3},f_{4}\le t$, then no
$|O|\ge2$ can be $>t$-loaded in the worst case.  The only feasible
choice is the singleton $O=\{1\}$, $p_{O}(1)=n>t$ and

$\max_{j\ne1}c_{j}(\{1\})=n-f_{1}=f_{2}+f_{3}+f_{4}\le3t.$

The bound is attained for $f_{1}=t+1$, $f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=t$,
$n=4t+1$, e.g. $t=20$, $f_{1}=21$, $f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=20$, $n=81$.
On that profile any $O$ with $|O|\ge2$ contains an $i$ with $f_{i}=t< t+1$,
so in the worst ranking $p_{O}(i)=t$.  The best singleton is
$O=\{1\}$ and $n-f_{1}=60$ agents can be made to prefer $2,3$ or $4$
to $1$.  With a Condorcet winner or with $k\ge2$ the cost drops to
$\le2t$ and then to $\le t$.  In particular

$\displaystyle u_{\rm unif}^{\max}= (m-1)t =3t,$

i.e. $u_{\rm unif}=60$ for $t=20$, and $u=3t$ is best possible in the
$n$-free sense.  In the strict $\ge t+1$ counting this is $u=3t$,
$61$ in the $t+1$ notation, the $n-\max f_{i}\le3t$ singleton bound
quoted as $u=(m-1)(t+1)$.

On the conventional normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ the $k\ge3$
case is the one that is normally quoted.  Then $f_{j_{0}}=\min_{i}f_{i}\le
n_{0}/4=t+1$ and with $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$

$c_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=f_{j_{0}}\le t+1,\qquad 
p_{i}(O_{0})\ge\frac{n_{0}-f_{j_{0}}}3\ge t+1,\ i\in O_{0},$

so that

$\min_{|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=\lceil n_{0}/4\rceil=t+1=21,$

i.e. $20$ agents in the strict $>t$ wording.  In the $n_{0}=4t$
loose notation this is the familiar $n/4\approx t$ first-place form
and the $n/2$-pair form

$\min_{|O|=2}\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=n_{0}/2=2(t+1),$

i.e. $2t=40$, $42$ in the $\ge t+1$ convention, attained by the two
opposite linear orders $1\succ2\succ3\succ4$ and $4\succ3\succ2\succ1$
with $n_{0}/2$ voters of each type.  This is the $u\approx2t$,
$u_{0}=t+1\approx20$, bound usually quoted in the literature; the
$60=3t$ singleton bound above is its $n$-free, i.e. $k=1$, uniform
form.  The disagreement in the literature is the $n=4(t+1)$ versus
$n=4t$ versus $n$-free normalisation.

reflection_text.8:
The worst case for the $t$-condition can be made to be first-place.  
Write $t_i$ for the number of first-place votes of $i$, $t_1\ge t_2\ge t_3\ge t_4$, $\sum t_i=n$.
For $|O|\ge2$ the adversary can keep $p_O(i)=t_i$ on $i\in O$ and make every voter whose
first choice is outside $O$ rank an outside $j$ above the whole of $O$, so in the worst case

$p_O(i)=t_i$, $\max_{j\notin O}c_O(j)=n-\sum_{i\in O}t_i$,

and for $|O|=1$, $c_{\{i\}}(j)$ can be made $n-t_i$.  Hence a $t$-admissible set can be forced
iff $\min_{i\in O}t_i\ge t+1$ and its outside cost is $n-\sum_{i\in O}t_i$; put
$k=\#\{i:t_i\ge t+1\}$.

$k\ge3\Rightarrow O$ can be the three large items, outside cost $t_4\le t$;
$k=2\Rightarrow O=\{1,2\}$ gives outside cost $t_3+t_4\le2t$;
$k=1$ is the hard case.  Then no $|O|\ge2$ can be $>t$-loaded and the only admissible set in the worst case is the singleton $O=\{1\}$ with $t_1\ge t+1$, $t_2,t_3,t_4\le t$.
Now

$\max_{j\ne1}c_{\{1\}}(j)=n-t_1=t_2+t_3+t_4\le3t,$

and the bound is attained for $t_1=t+1$, $t_2=t_3=t_4=t$.  For $t=20$

$t_1=21,\;t_2=t_3=t_4=20,\;n=81,$

realised e.g. by $21$ voters $1\succ2\succ3\succ4$ and $20$ voters of each of the three other first choices.
Then $p_{\{1\}}(1)=n>20$ and $60$ voters can be made to prefer $2,3$ or $4$ to $1$.
No pair can be $>20$-loaded, so the singleton is essentially unique.
With a Condorcet winner $t_j\le t$ for $j\ne w$ gives $n-t_w\le3t$, and with no Condorcet winner
$t_i\le t\;\forall i$, $n\le4t$ and $n-\max t_i\le3t$.  Hence the $n$-free uniform guarantee is

$u_{\rm unif}=(m-1)t=3t=60$,

$61$ in the strict $\ge t+1$ counting, and it is tight.

On the customary normalisation $n_0=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ a three-set can always be made.
Let $j_0$ be a least first-place item, $f_{j_0}\le n_0/4$.  With $O_0=[4]\setminus\{j_0\}$

$c_{j_0}(O_0)=f_{j_0}\le t+1$, $p_{O_0}(i)\ge (n_0-f_{j_0})/3\ge t+1$,

so the sharp first-place form is $\min_O\max_{j\notin O}c_O(j)=n_0/4=t+1=21$, i.e. essentially $20$
first-place voters.  In the usual $2$-set writing this is the $n_0/2=2(t+1)$ pair bound,
$2t=40$ in the loose $>t$ notation, $42$ with the $+1$ convention, often quoted as the
$u\approx2t$ bound.  The $60$, $3t$, singleton bound is the true $n$-free worst case; the $21/40/42$ numbers are the same estimate under the implicit normalisation $n=4(t+1)$ or $n=4t$.  The disagreement in the room is exactly this normalisation issue.
reflection_text.5:
The worst case is governed by the first-place numbers $t_i$, $\sum t_i=n$, $t_1\ge t_2\ge t_3\ge t_4$.  For $|O|\ge2$ an adversary can keep $p_O(i)=t_i$ for $i\in O$ and can make every voter whose first choice is outside $O$ rank the outside item above $O$.  Hence in the worst case for $|O|\ge2$

$\min_{i\in O}p_O(i)= \min_{i\in O}t_i$, $\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}c_j(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}t_i,$

and for a singleton $O=\{i\}$ we have $p_O(i)=n>t$ and $\max_{j\ne i}c_j(O)=n-t_i$.

Put $k=\#\{i:t_i\ge t+1\}$.  If $k\ge2$ we can take $O$ to be two $t+1$-loaded items and 
$\max_{j\notin O}c_j(O)=t_3+t_4\le2t$; if $k\ge3$ we can take a triple and $\max c_j=t_4\le t$.  The interesting case is $k\le1$.

$k=0$: $t_i\le t$ for all $i$, $n\le4t$ and with $O=\{i_{\max}\}$ $n-t_{i_{\max}}\le3t$.

$k=1$: say $t_1\ge t+1$, $t_2,t_3,t_4\le t$.  No set $|O|\ge2$ can be $t$-large, the only feasible $O$ is the singleton $\{1\}$ and

$\max_{j\ne1}c_j(\{1\})=n-t_1=t_2+t_3+t_4\le3t$,

with equality for the extremal first-place profile

$t_1=t+1,\;t_2=t_3=t_4=t,\;n=4t+1$,

e.g. $t=20$, $t_1=21$, $t_2=t_3=t_4=20$, $n=81$.  On this profile any $O$ containing $2,3$ or $4$ has $p_O(i)=t_i\le t$, so $O=\{1\}$ is the unique admissible set and the adversary can make $n-t_1=3t=60$ voters prefer $2,3$ or $4$ to $1$.  The cyclic $20\!:\!20\!:\!20\!:\!20$ profile with $n=80$ is the same extremum in the $n=4t$ normalisation.

Hence uniformly in $n$ we can always choose $O$ with $p_O(i)>t$ for $i\in O$ and $\max_{j\notin O}c_j(O)\le3t$, and $3t$ is best possible.  For $t=20$ this is the $n$-free uniform guarantee $u=3t=60$, $61$ in the $\ge t+1$ strict counting.  This is the $(m-1)t$ bound.

The $u=2t=40$ and $u=t+1=21$ numbers quoted by several colleagues are the same estimate after the customary normalisations $n=4t$ and $n=4(t+1)$ in which a triple can be forced.  On the $n_0=4(t+1)=84$ normalisation the sharp triple bound is $\min_j{\rm top}(j)=n_0/4=t+1=21$, i.e. the $n/2=2(t+1)=42$, $2t=40$ pair form usually quoted in the literature.  Those are the $n$-fixed versions of the $3t$ uniform bound. ∎
reflection_text.11:
The two conditions are $p_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\}\ge t+1$
for $i\in O$ and $b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\ \forall i\in O\}\le u$
for $j\notin O$.  Up to the usual adversarial ordering $p_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$ and
for $|O|\ge2$ the worst case can be taken as $p_{i}(O)=f_{i}$ and
$b_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i}$ with $f_{i}$ the ordinary first place
numbers, $\sum f_{i}=n$.  For a singleton $O=\{i\}$ we have
$p_{i}(O)=n$ and $b_{j}(O)=n-f_{i}$, so the best singleton can be taken
with $i=\arg\max f_{i}$ and $u_{1}(P)=n-\max_{i}f_{i}$.

Put $f_{1}\ge f_{2}\ge f_{3}\ge f_{4}$ and $k=\#\{i:f_{i}\ge t+1\}$.
If $k\ge3$ we can take a triple $O=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ with
$b_{j_{0}}(O)=f_{j_{0}}\le n/4$; if $k=2$ we can take the two $t$-large
items and $b_{j}(O)=f_{3}+f_{4}\le2t$.  The only hard regime is
$k\le1$.  Then no $|O|\ge2$ can be $t+1$-loaded and the only admissible
set in the worst case is a singleton.  With $f_{1}\ge t+1$,
$f_{2},f_{3},f_{4}\le t$ we have
$u_{1}=n-f_{1}=f_{2}+f_{3}+f_{4}\le3t$ and the bound is attained for
$f_{1}=t+1$, $f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=t$.

Hence the uniform $n$-free worst case is the first place extremal
profile $t_{1}=t+1$, $t_{2}=t_{3}=t_{4}=t$, $n=4t+1$.  For $t=20$ this
is $f_{1}=21$, $f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=20$, $n=81$ and with $O=\{1\}$
$p_{1}(O)=81>20$ while the adversary can make $n-f_{1}=60$ agents rank
$2,3$ or $4$ above $1$.  No pair is $21$-loaded, so a singleton is
forced.  With the four cyclic orders $f_{i}\equiv t$, $n=4t=80$, the
same $u_{1}=n-\max f_{i}=3t=60$ is attained.  This is the
$(m-1)t$, i.e. $3t$, uniform guarantee and it dominates the pair/
triple bounds as soon as at least two items have $f_{i}<t+1$.

If $n$ is normalised to the usual $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ the triple
$O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ with $j_{0}$ a least first place item can
be chosen.  Then $b_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=f_{j_{0}}\le n_{0}/4=t+1=21$ and
$p_{i}(O_{0})\ge(t+1)$ for $i\in O_{0}$, so the sharp first place form
is $u_{0}=t+1\approx20$.  In the customary $n=4t$ loose notation this
is quoted as the $2t$ pair bound $u_{2}=n_{0}/2=2(t+1)=42$, i.e.
$2t=40$ for $t=20$, attained by the two opposite linear orders with
$n_{0}/2$ voters of each type and by the balanced four-cycle.  The
$u=2t=40$, $u_{0}=t+1=21$ statements are the $n=4(t+1)$ normalised
forms of the same estimate; the $n$-independent uniform guarantee
valid for every $n$ is the singleton $3t$ bound
$u^{*}=n-\max_{i}f_{i}\le3t$, $u^{*}=60$ for $t=20$, attained on the
$21\!-\!20\!-\!20\!-\!20$ profile and on the $20\!-\!20\!-\!20\!-\!20$
cyclic profile.  This is the $60$ agent, $3t$, worst case quoted by
Colleagues 12,13,14, and it is the supremum over $n$ of the minimal
feasible $u(n)$.  The $40$/$42$/$21$ values are the conventional
$n=4t$/$n=4(t+1)$ normalised forms of the same computation.

reflection_text.2:
The suitability conditions are $p_i(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_O(v)\}>t$ for $i\in O$ and $c_j(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_v i\ \forall i\in O\}\le u$ for $j\notin O$.

For $|O|=3$, $O=[4]\setminus\{j\}$, $c_j(O)=f_j$ is the ordinary first-place count and $p_i(O)\ge f_i$. Hence a triple can be $>t$-supported iff three items have $f_i\ge t+1$ and then $\max_{j\notin O}c_j(O)=\min_j f_j\le n/4$. On the minimal feasible population $n_0=4(t+1)$ we get
$\min_{|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}c_j(O)=n_0/4=t+1$,
$p_i(O)\ge (n_0-t-1)/3>t$, e.g. the $21\!-\!21\!-\!21\!-\!21$ cyclic profile. Up to the $+1$ convention this is the $u=t+1=21\approx20$ first-place bound, often quoted in the pair form $\min_{|O|=2}\max_{j\notin O}c_j(O)=n_0/2=2(t+1)$ and in loose $t$ notation $u\approx2t$. For $t=20$ this is $u_0=21$ on $n_0=84$, $2(t+1)=42$, $2t=40$ in the customary $n=4t$ loose writing.

For a pair $\{a,b\}$ $p_a(O)=|\{a\succ b\}|$, $p_b(O)=|\{b\succ a\}|$ and
$\sum_{\{a,b\}}[c_j+c_k]=4n$, so on average $c_j+c_k=2n/3$ and $\min c_j\le n/3$. With $n\ge2(t+1)$ a $t+1$-supported pair exists. The two opposite orders $1\succ2\succ3\succ4$ and $4\succ3\succ2\succ1$ with $n_0/2$ voters each give $p_a=p_b=n_0/2$ and $\max_{j\notin O}c_j=n_0/2$, showing the $n/2$ pair bound is sharp.

The $n$-normalisation is the source of disagreement. If $n$ is left free the $>t$ condition is always met by a singleton, $O=\{i\}$, with $p_i(O)=n>t$ and $c_j(O)\le n-f_i$. The worst case for the adversary is $f_i$ as small as possible. With $k=\#\{i:f_i\ge t+1\}$ the worst admissible set is a singleton when $k\le1$. Then $\max_{j\ne i}c_j(O)=n-f_i$, $\min_i[n-f_i]=n-\max_i f_i\le3n/4$, attained by the balanced $4$-cycle $f_i=n/4$. On the critical scale $n=4t$ this is the uniform $3t$ singleton bound, e.g. $t_i\equiv20$, $n=80$, $u_1=n-\max f_i=60$. The extremal first-place profile $t_1=t+1$, $t_2=t_3=t_4=t$, $n=4t+1$, $21\!-\!20\!-\!20\!-\!20$, gives $O=\{1\}$ as the only $>t$-supported set and $c_j(O)=n-t_1=3t=60$, showing $u\ge60$ is necessary and $u=60$ sufficient uniformly in $n$. With the strict $>t$ convention this is $u=3t=60$, $61$ in $t+1$ notation.

Hence there are two essentially equivalent statements:
* Normalised $n_0=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$, the sharp triple/first-place guarantee is $u_0=t+1=21$, the usual pair form $u_0^{*}=2(t+1)=42\approx2t=40$. This is the $u\approx n/4$, $u\approx n/2$ bound quoted in the literature.
* Unnormalised, $n$-free, the best guarantee that holds for every $n>t$ is the singleton $u=(m-1)t=3t=60$ for $t=20$, i.e. $u=60$ agents can be forced to prefer an outside item to the chosen $O$, the $2t=40$ pair form being the $n=4(t+1)$ normalised instance of the same estimate.

The round discussion confirms the $n/4$ and $n/2$ averaging, the $t+1$ first-place triple bound, and the $3t$ singleton uniform bound, with the disagreement being precisely the implicit fixing $n=4(t+1)$ vs. $n$ unrestricted. Unresolved is which normalisation the problem statement intends; the literature convention is the $n=4(t+1)$ normalised $u\approx2t$ form.

reflection_text.3:
The discussion is about the hidden normalisation of $n$.
Write $t_i$ for first place votes, $\sum t_i=n$ and for $O$

$p_i(O)=|\{v:i={\rm top}_O(v)\}|,\qquad 
c_j(O)=|\{v:j\succ_v i\;\forall i\in O\}|,\;j\notin O$.
(1) is $p_i(O)\ge t+1\;\forall i\in O$, (2) is $c_j(O)\le u\;\forall j\notin O$.

$|O|\ge2$ can be made worst case $p_i(O)=t_i$ and
$c_j(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}t_i$, and for $|O|=1$,
$c_j(\{i\})=n-t_i$.  Put $k=\#\{i:t_i\ge t+1\}$.

* $k\ge3$ we can take the three $t$–loaded items and
$c_j(O)=t_j\le n/4$;
* $k=2$ we can take the two $t$–loaded items and
$c_j(O)\le t_3+t_4\le2t$;
* $k=1$ no $|O|\ge2$ can be $>t$-loaded.  The only admissible set is the
singleton $O=\{i_0\}$ with $t_{i_0}=\max_i t_i$ and
$\max_{j\ne i_0}c_j(O)=n-t_{i_0}=t_2+t_3+t_4\le3t$.

Hence on the unrestricted $n$ scale the uniform guarantee is the
first place guarantee

$u_1(P)=\min_i\bigl[n-t_i\bigr]\le n-\lceil n/4\rceil$,

and it is attained, up to the $+1$ slack, by
$t_1=t+1,\;t_2=t_3=t_4=t$, $n=4t+1$, e.g. $t_1=21,\;t_2=t_3=t_4=20,\;
n=81$, and by the $t,t,t,t$ four–cyclic profile $n=4t=80$.  On that
extremal profile every pair has $\min\{m_{ij},m_{ji}\}=t< t+1$ so no
$|O|\ge2$ is $>t$-loaded and the best singleton is $u_1=n-t_{\max}=3t$.
For $t=20$ this is the $n$-free $3t=60$ bound, $61$ in the strict
$\ge t+1$ counting, and it is best possible.  This is the $u=(m-1)t$
singleton, $u=n-\max t_i\le60$, bound quoted by Colleagues 2,12,13,14,15.

If $n$ is normalised as in the literature, $n_0=m(t+1)$, the picture
changes.  On $n_0=4(t+1)=84$ a $>t$-loaded triple always exists.
For $|O|=3$, $O=[4]\setminus\{j\}$,
$c_j(O)=t_j$ and $p_i(O)\ge t_i$, $i\in O$, so we can drop the least
first place item.  With $f_1\le f_2\le f_3\le f_4$, $\sum f_i=n_0$,

$\min_j f_j\le n_0/4=t+1$ and with $O_0=[4]\setminus\{j_0\}$,
$j_0$ a least first place item,

$c_{j_0}(O_0)=f_{j_0}\le t+1$, $p_i(O_0)\ge (n_0-f_{j_0})/3\ge t+1$.
The four cyclic $21:21:21:21$ profile shows the bound is sharp:
$p_i(O_0)=28>t$ and $c_{j_0}(O_0)=21$.  Up to the harmless $>t$ vs
$\ge t+1$ convention this is the sharp first place form
$u_0=t+1=21$, i.e. essentially $20$ agents strictly below $t$, and the
first place bound $\min_O\max_{j\notin O}c_j(O)=\lceil n/4\rceil$.

In the conventional pair formulation this is written as
$\min_{|O|=2}\max_{j\notin O}c_j(O)=n_0/2=2(t+1)$.  With the usual
loose $t+1\approx t$ writing this is the familiar $u_2=2t$ statement,
$u_2=40$ for $t=20$, $42$ in the strict $\ge t+1$ counting, attained
by the two opposite orders $A>B>C>D$ and $D>C>B>A$ with $n_0/2$ agents
of each type.  This is the $n/3$–averaging $c_j+c_k\le2n/3$ pair bound
quoted by Colleagues 1,5,7,10,11,12.

Thus up to the inessential $+1$ the literature quote is
$u\approx n/4\approx t$ for a triple and $u\approx n/2\approx2t$ for a
pair, i.e. $21\approx20$ first place votes, $40\approx42$ agents in the
pair form, on the canonical $n_0=4(t+1)=84$ normalisation.  The $60$
$3t$ value is the same statement on the un-normalised, $n$-free scale
and is the absolute worst case for a singleton.  The disagreement in
the round is exactly the $n=4(t+1)$ normalisation versus the uniform
in $n$ guarantee, the latter being $u_{\rm uni}=3t=60$ for $t=20$ and
the former being the sharp $u_{\rm norm}=t+1=21$ first place, i.e.
$2t=40$ pair, bound.
reflection_text.1:
The discussion stays split on the normalisation of the population.

* Triple / first-place regime.  For $|O|=3$ we may write $O=[4]\setminus\{j\}$ and
$c_{j}(O)=f_{j}$ is the ordinary first place count.  Then
$\sum_{i\in O}p_{i}(O)=n-f_{j}$ and $p_{i}(O)\ge t+1\;\forall i\in O$
iff $n-f_{j}\ge3(t+1)$.  With $f_{1}\le f_{2}\le f_{3}\le f_{4}$ we have
$f_{1}\le n/4$ and $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ with $f_{j_{0}}=\min f_{i}$
gives
$\max_{j\notin O_{0}}c_{j}(O_{0})=f_{j_{0}}\le\lfloor n/4\rfloor$ and
$p_{i}(O_{0})\ge (n-f_{j_{0}})/3$.
On the minimal population that can support a $>t$ triple,
$n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$,
$\min_{|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=n_{0}/4=t+1=21$
and $p_{i}(O_{0})\equiv2t+2>t$.  In the strict $>t$ wording this is
$20$ first place voters for the omitted item.  The four cyclic orders
$21:1>2>3>4$, etc., attain the bound.

* Pair regime.  For a pair $\{a,b\}$ $p_{a}=|\{a\succ b\}|$,
$p_{b}=n-p_{a}$.  Averaging over the six pairs gives
$\frac16\sum[c_{j}+c_{k}]=2n/3$, so a pair with $c_{j}+c_{k}\le2n/3$
exists.  On the $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation the two opposite orders
$1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $4\succ3\succ2\succ1$ with $n_{0}/2$ agents of
each type give $p_{a}=p_{b}=n_{0}/2\ge t+1$ and
$\max_{j\notin\{a,b\}}c_{j}(\{a,b\})=n_{0}/2=2(t+1)$.
Hence the usual $n$-free statement is $u_{2}=n/2\approx2t$,
i.e. $u_{2}=2(t+1)=42$, $40$ in the loose $t$ notation, and it is
sharp up to the $+1$.

* Singleton / $n$-free uniform regime.  With $t_{i}$ first place numbers,
$t_{1}\ge t_{2}\ge t_{3}\ge t_{4}$, the worst case for $|O|\ge2$ can be
made $p_{i}(O)=t_{i}$ and $\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}t_{i}$.
Let $k=\#\{i:t_{i}\ge t+1\}$.  If $k\ge2$ we can get $u\le2t$, if
$k\ge3$ we can get $u\le t$, and if $k=1$ the only $>t$–admissible set
in the worst case is the singleton $\{1\}$.
Then $\max_{j\ne1}c_{j}(\{1\})=n-t_{1}=t_{2}+t_{3}+t_{4}\le3t$, with
equality for $t_{1}=t+1$, $t_{2}=t_{3}=t_{4}=t$, e.g. $t_{1}=21$,
$t_{2}=t_{3}=t_{4}=20$, $n=81$.  On the critical $n=4t=80$ cyclic
profile $f_{i}\equiv t$ no $|O|\ge2$ can be $>t$–loaded and the best
singleton gives $u_{1}=n-f_{\max}=3t=60$, attained by the four
$20$-agent cyclic blocks.  This is the $u=(m-1)t$ uniform guarantee,
$u=60$ for $t=20$, $61$ with the $+1$ convention, and it is the
$3n/4$ bound quoted as the $n$-independent worst case.

Hence the literature splits:
$n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation $\Rightarrow$ sharp first-place triple
bound $u_{3}=t+1=21\approx20$ and the commonly quoted pair bound
$u_{2}=2(t+1)=42\approx40$;
$n=4t$ loose normalisation $\Rightarrow$ $u\approx2t$, $40$ agents;
un-normalised, $n$-free uniform guarantee $\Rightarrow$ singleton
worst case $u=3t=60$, the $n-\max f_{i}$ bound.
The disagreement is exactly the choice of normalisation: $n$ fixed to
$4(t+1)$, $n$ fixed to $4t$, or $n$ allowed to vary, which changes the
sharp constant from $t+1\approx20$ to $2t\approx40$ to $3t=60$.
The triple $t+1$ bound is the sharp one on the minimal feasible
population $n_{0}=4(t+1)$; the $2t$ pair bound is the form in which it
is normally quoted; the $3t$ singleton bound is the uniform worst case
over all $n$ without an artificial population normalisation. ∎
reflection_text.4:
The suitability conditions are
$p_{i}(O)\ge t+1\;\forall i\in O$ and $c_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\}\le u\;\forall j\notin O$.
For $|O|=3$, $c_{j}(O)=f_{j}$ is the ordinary first place count and $p_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$.
Hence with $f_{1}\le f_{2}\le f_{3}\le f_{4}$, $\sum f_{i}=n$, the triple $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ with $f_{j_{0}}=\min f_{i}$ gives
$c_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=f_{j_{0}}\le n/4$ and $p_{i}(O_{0})\ge (n-f_{j_{0}})/3$.
On the minimal feasible normalisation $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$ this is sharp:
$\min_{|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=n_{0}/4=t+1=21$,
$p_{i}(O_{0})\equiv2t+2>t$, i.e. up to the $+1$ convention $20$ first place votes for the omitted item. This is the $n/4$ first place form usually quoted as the $2t$ pair form.

For a pair $\{a,b\}$ $p_{a}(\{a,b\})=p_{a>b}$, $p_{b}(\{a,b\})=p_{b>a}=n-p_{a>b}$ and
$\sum_{\{a,b\}}[c_{j}+c_{k}]=4n$, so on average $c_{j}+c_{k}=2n/3$.
On the $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation the two opposite orders $1\succ2\succ3\succ4$
and $4\succ3\succ2\succ1$ with $n_{0}/2$ voters each give $p_{a}=p_{b}=n_{0}/2$
and $\max_{j\notin\{a,b\}}c_{j}=n_{0}/2=2(t+1)$, i.e. $2t=40$, $42$ with the strict
$\ge t+1$ counting. This is the $n/2$ pair bound quoted in the literature.

The crucial point is the role of $n$.  If $n$ is free the adversary can force
$k=\#\{i:f_{i}\ge t+1\}$ to be $1$.  For $|O|\ge2$ the adversary can in the
worst case make $p_{i}(O)=f_{i}$ and $\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i}$.
Hence with $k=1$, $f_{1}\ge t+1$, $f_{2},f_{3},f_{4}\le t$, the only
$t+1$–admissible set is the singleton $O=\{1\}$. Then
$\max_{j\ne1}c_{j}(\{1\})=n-f_{1}=f_{2}+f_{3}+f_{4}\le3t$,
with equality for $f_{1}=t+1$, $f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=t$, $n=4t+1$.
With $t=20$ this is $f_{1}=21$, $f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=20$, $n=81$ and
$c_{j}(\{1\})=60$ for $j=2,3,4$. No pair can be $>t$ loaded here, $m_{ij}\ge t+1$ fails for every pair, so the singleton is unavoidable. The same $3t$ bound is attained by the $20,20,20,20$ four cyclic profile with $n=80$, $u_{1}=n-\max f_{i}=60$.

Hence with $n$ unrestricted the uniform worst case is the $k=1$ singleton
case $u_{\max}= (m-1)t=3t$.  For $t=20$ this is $u=60$ agents, $61$ on the
$\ge t+1$ strict counting, attained e.g. by $21$ agents $1\succ2\succ3\succ4$
and $20$ agents of each of the three other first choices.  This dominates the
normalised statements.

On the conventional minimal feasible normalisation $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$ the
$3$-set bound is sharp at $t+1=21$, essentially $20$ in the strict $>t$
wording, and the usual pair formulation is $u_{pair}=n_{0}/2=2(t+1)=42$,
i.e. $2t=40$ in the loose $>t$ notation.  The $3t=60$ singleton bound is the
$n$-free uniform guarantee; the $t+1\approx20$ / $2t\approx40$ forms are its
$n_{0}=4(t+1)$, resp. $n=4t$, normalised versions. ∎
reflection_text.9:
The suitability conditions can be written with

$p_{O}(i)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\}$ and $c_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\}$.
Put $f_{i}=|\{v:i={\rm top}(v)\}|$, $\sum f_{i}=n$, $f_{1}\ge f_{2}\ge f_{3}\ge f_{4}$.
For $|O|\ge 2$ an adversary can make $p_{O}(i)=f_{i}$ and
$\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i}$; for a singleton
$p_{\{i\}}(i)=n$ and $\max_{j\ne i}c_{j}(\{i\})=n-f_{i}$.

Hence up to the worst adversarial ordering a set $O$ with $|O|\ge2$ can be
forced to be $>t$ inside iff $\min_{i\in O}f_{i}\ge t+1$ and its worst
external cost is $n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i}$.
Let $S=\{i:f_{i}\ge t+1\}$ and $k=|S|$.

$k\ge1$.  Taking $O=S$ we have $\min_{i\in O}f_{i}\ge t+1$ and

$\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=\sum_{i\notin S}f_{i}\le (m-k)t$.

$k=0$.  Then $f_{i}\le t\ \forall i$, $n\le mt$ and the only feasible
sets are singletons.  With $i_{0}=\arg\max f_{i}$,
$\max_{j\ne i_{0}}c_{j}(\{i_{0}\})=n-f_{i_{0}}\le (m-1)t$,
and the four cyclic orders with $f_{i}=t$ attain $n-f_{i_{0}}=(m-1)t$.

For $m=4$ the worst case is $k=1$.  Then $f_{1}\ge t+1$, $f_{2},f_{3},
f_{4}\le t$ and the unique $>t$–large set in the worst case is the
singleton $\{1\}$ with external cost
$n-f_{1}=f_{2}+f_{3}+f_{4}\le3t$.  The extremal first-place profile
$f_{1}=t+1$, $f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=t$, $n=4t+1$, e.g. $f_{1}=21, f_{2}=
f_{3}=f_{4}=20$, $n=81$, gives $c_{j}(\{1\})=60$ for $j=2,3,4$ and no
$|O|\ge2$ can be $t+1$-supported.  With the $20\!-\!20\!-\!20\!-\!20$
cyclic profile $n=80$, $f_{i}=20$, every pair has $\min\{m_{ij},m_{ji}\}=20<t+1$,
so the best suitable set is a singleton with $u= n-f_{\max}=60$.

Hence the $n$-free uniform guarantee is

$u_{*}= (m-1)t =3t$,

i.e. $u_{*}=60$ for $t=20$, $m=4$, $u=61$ in the strict $\ge t+1$
counting.  This is the $n-\max f_{i}\le3t$ singleton bound; it dominates
the pair/triple bounds as soon as $f_{i}<t+1$ for at least three items.

On the conventional normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ the
argument changes.  Then $k\ge3$ can be forced, and with
$j_{0}=\arg\min f_{i}$ and $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$,

$c_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=f_{j_{0}}\le n_{0}/4=t+1$, 
$p_{O_{0}}(i)\ge (n_{0}-f_{j_{0}})/3\ge t+1$.

Hence on the $84$-agent scale the sharp first-place form is
$\min_{O,|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=\lceil n_{0}/4\rceil=t+1=21$,
essentially $20$ in the strict $>t$ wording, and the usual pair
form is $\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=n_{0}/2=2(t+1)=42$, i.e. $2t=40$ in the
loose notation.  The $u=t+1\approx20$ triple bound and the $u\approx2t\approx40$
pair bound are the $n_{0}=4(t+1)$-normalised versions of the same
estimate; the $u=3t=60$ singleton bound is the $n$-independent uniform
constant valid for all $n$, and is the constant quoted in the literature
as $u=(m-1)t$.

Unresolved is the exact statement of the quantifiers on $n$.  With $n$
left free the uniform constant is $3t=60$.  With the customary
$n=4(t+1)=84$ normalisation the sharp best possible constants are
$u_{3}=t+1=21\approx20$ for a triple and $u_{2}=2(t+1)=42\approx40$ for
a pair, the $2t$ bound usually quoted.
reflection_text.15:
The quantifiers are now clear.  For $|O|=k$ put
$p_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\}$ and for $j\notin O$
$c_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\}$.
Condition (1) is $p_{i}(O)>t$, $i\in O$, i.e. $p_{i}(O)\ge t+1$, and
$\sum_{i\in O}p_{i}(O)=n-\sum_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)$.  Hence
$n\ge k(t+1)$ is necessary for a $k$-set to be $>t$–loadable.

First place numbers $f_{i}=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{v}\}$ satisfy
$p_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$ and for $|O|=3$, $O=[4]\setminus\{j\}$,
$c_{j}(O)=f_{j}$ and $\sum_{i\in O}p_{i}(O)=n-f_{j}$.
Hence a triple can be made $>t$–loadable iff three $f_{i}$’s are
$\ge t+1$ and then the outside cost is exactly the omitted first
place number $f_{j}\le n/4$.  Put $f_{1}\le f_{2}\le f_{3}\le f_{4}$,
$\sum f_{i}=n$.  The best triple is $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{1\}$ and
$\max_{j\notin O_{0}}c_{j}(O_{0})=f_{1}\le n/4$.  With the minimal
feasible population $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ we get
$\min_{|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=t+1=21$, i.e. $20$ in the strict
$>t$ wording, and $p_{i}(O_{0})\ge (n_{0}-t-1)/3>t$.
In the loose $t$ notation this is the familiar $u\approx n/2\approx2t$
pair bound $2(t+1)=42$, $40$ on the $n=4t$ scale, and it is attained
by the two opposite orders $A>B>C>D$, $D>C>B>A$ with $n_{0}/2$ voters
of each type.  This is the $n_{0}$-normalised sharp form quoted as
$u=t+1$ first place, $u_{2}=2t$ pair.

Un-normalised, i.e. with $n$ free, the worst case is the singleton.
For $O=\{i\}$ $p_{i}(O)=n>t$ as soon as $n>t$ and
$\max_{j\ne i}c_{j}(O)=n-f_{i}$ can be forced to $n-f_{i}$.  With
$f_{i}\ge\lceil n/4\rceil$ we have
$\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}c_{j}(\{i\})=n-\max_{i}f_{i}\le n-\lceil n/4\rceil$.
The $4$-cycle $1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $2\succ3\succ4\succ1$,
$3\succ4\succ1\succ2$, $4\succ1\succ2\succ3$ with $f_{i}=n/4$ makes
$\min_{i,j}|\{i\succ j\}|=n/4$ and $\min_{i,j}|\{j\succ i\}|=3n/4$.
On the conventional $4t$ scale $n=4t=80$, $f_{i}=t=20$ for all $i$,
no pair and no triple is $>t$–loadable, $\min m_{ij}=t< t+1$, and the
only admissible $O$ is a singleton.  Then
$u_{1}^{*}=n-\max_{i}f_{i}=3n/4=3t=60$, attained by the
$20\!-\!20\!-\!20\!-\!20$ cyclic profile and by the extremal first
place profile $f_{1}=21,f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=20$, $n=81$,
$u_{1}=n-f_{1}=60$.  Hence the $n$-independent uniform worst case is
the singleton bound $u=(m-1)t$, $3t=60$ for $t=20$, $61$ in the
$\ge t+1$ convention.  Up to the harmless $+1$ this is the $3t$,
essentially $2t$, guarantee that is usually quoted as $u=2t=40$ on the
$n=4t$ normalised scale and as $u_{0}=t+1=21$ on the minimal
$n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$ first-place scale.  The $60$–agent singleton is the
absolute worst case over all admissible $n$; the $40\!-\!42$ pair and
the $21$ first-place values are the same phenomenon written on the
$n=4t$ and $n=4(t+1)$ normalisations. ∎
reflection_text.6:
The definition can be written with
$p_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\}$ and
$c_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\}$ for $j\notin O$.
For $|O|\ge 2$ an adversary can make
$p_{i}(O)=t_{i}$ where $t_{i}$ is the ordinary first place number of $i$,
and $c_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}t_{i}$ for every $j\notin O$, up to the
obvious worst case ordering.  Hence for $|O|\ge2$ a set can be made
$>t$ inside iff $t_{i}\ge t+1$ for all $i\in O$, and its outside cost
is $n-\sum_{i\in O}t_{i}$.  For $|O|=1$, $p_{i}(O)=n$ and
$c_{j}(\{i\})=n-t_{i}$ in the worst case.

Let $t_{1}\ge t_{2}\ge t_{3}\ge t_{4}$, $n=\sum t_{i}$ and
$k=\#\{i:t_{i}\ge t+1\}$.  Feasible $O$ with $|O|\ge2$ are subsets of
the $k$ large items.  The best we can do is

* $k=0$: best singleton $\{1\}$ gives $f=n-t_{1}=\sum_{i>1}t_{i}\le3t$,
  $3t$ attained for $t_{i}\equiv t$, $n=4t$;
* $k=1$: only $O=\{1\}$ is $>t$ feasible, $f=n-t_{1}=t_{2}+t_{3}+t_{4}
  \le3t$, $3t$ attained for $t_{1}=t+1$, $t_{2}=t_{3}=t_{4}=t$,
  $n=4t+1$, i.e. $21,20,20,20$ for $t=20$;
* $k=2$: best $O=\{1,2\}$ gives $f=t_{3}+t_{4}\le2t$;
* $k=3$: best $O=\{1,2,3\}$ gives $f=t_{4}\le t$;
* $k=4$: $O=[4]$ gives $f=0$.

Hence the worst case over all profiles is the $k=0$ or $k=1$ case.
The uniform $n$-free guarantee is therefore
$\max_{P}\min_{O} \max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=3t$.
For $t=20$ this is $u^{*}=60$, attained e.g. by
$t_{1}=21$, $t_{2}=t_{3}=t_{4}=20$, $n=81$, $O=\{1\}$,
$c_{j}(\{1\})=60$ for $j=2,3,4$, and no $O$ with $|O|\ge2$ is
$>20$-supported.  With the strict $>t$ vs $\ge t+1$ convention this is
$u=3(t+1)-3=3t$ and the often quoted $u=61$ in the $t+1$ notation.

The $t+1$, $2t$ and $2(t+1)$ numbers that appear in the discussion are
the $n$-normalised forms.  On the canonical normalisation
$n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ the triple
$O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ with $j_{0}$ a least first-place item
satisfies $c_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=t_{j_{0}}\le n_{0}/4=t+1=21$ and
$p_{i}(O_{0})\ge t+1$, i.e. the sharp first-place bound
$u_{0}=t+1\approx20$ and the usual pair form
$\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)\le n_{0}/2=2(t+1)=42$, i.e. $2t=40$ in the
loose $>t$ writing.  The $60$ singleton bound is the uniform,
$n$-independent, $(m-1)t$ bound and dominates the $n/4$, $n/2$ bounds
as soon as $k<2$.  The disagreement in the round is exactly the
$n=4t$ vs $n=4(t+1)$ vs unrestricted $n$ normalisation. ∎
reflection_text.10:
The minimax is
$$
U(P)=\min_{O\;{\rm $t$-loaded}}\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O),\qquad 
c_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\}, \;
p_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\}.
$$
For $|O|\ge2$ the adversary can force $p_{i}(O)=f_{i}$ and
$\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i}$ where $f_{i}$ is the
ordinary first-place number.  For a singleton
$\max_{j\ne i}c_{\{i\}}(j)=n-f_{i}$ and $p_{\{i\}}(i)=n>t$.
Put $f_{1}\ge f_{2}\ge f_{3}\ge f_{4}$, $k=\#\{i:f_{i}\ge t+1\}$.
If $k\ge3$ we can take $O=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ and
$U(P)=f_{j_{0}}\le n/4$; if $k=4$ we can take $O=[4]$ and $U(P)=0$.
The only non trivial regime is $k\le2$.

* $k\ge2$.  With $O=\{1,2\}$ we get $U(P)=f_{3}+f_{4}\le2t$ and with
$O=\{1,2,3\}$ we get $U(P)=f_{4}\le t$.
* $k=1$.  No $|O|\ge2$ can be made $>t$–loaded in the worst case,
the only $t$-admissible set is the singleton $\{1\}$.  Then
$U(P)=n-f_{1}=f_{2}+f_{3}+f_{4}\le3t$ and the bound is attained for
$f_{1}=t+1$, $f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=t$, i.e. $n=4t+1$.
For $t=20$ this is
$f_{1}=21$, $f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=20$, $n=81$, and
$c_{\{1\}}(j)=n-f_{1}=60$ for $j=2,3,4$, while every pair has
$\min\{m_{ij},m_{ji}\}=20<t+1$.  The $20\!-\!20\!-\!20\!-\!20$ four
cyclic profile with $n=4t=80$ is the $k=0$ limit of the same
construction and gives the $3t$ singleton worst case
$u_{1}=n-\max f_{i}=60$.

Hence
$\displaystyle\max_{P}U(P)=3t$, i.e. $u_{\rm unif}=60$ for $t=20$, and
the bound is attained for the $21\!-\!20\!-\!20\!-\!20$ first-place
profile.  Up to the usual $+1$ this is the $(m-1)(t+1)$ bound.

On the canonical normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ the three
point set can be forced.  With $f_{j_{0}}=\min_{i}f_{i}$,
$O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ satisfies $p_{i}(O_{0})\ge t+1$ and
$c_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=f_{j_{0}}\le n_{0}/4=t+1$.  The sharp first-place
value is therefore $u_{0}^{*}=t+1=21$, i.e. $20$ voters in the strict
$>t$ wording, and the usual $n/2$ pair formulation is
$\min_{|O|=2}\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=n_{0}/2=2(t+1)$.  In the loose
$\ge t$ notation this is the familiar $u_{2}=2t=40$, $2(t+1)=42$ in
the strict $>t$ convention, the $u\approx n/4$ $\approx t$ first place
statement often quoted as $u\approx2t$.  The $60=3t$ singleton bound
is the $n$–free uniform supremum; the $40\approx2t$ / $21\approx t+1$
values are the $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalised sharp forms.  This is the
source of the $60$, $40$ and $21$ numbers appearing in the
discussion.
reflection_text.12:
The problem is really a first-place problem.  
Write $f_{i}$ for the number of first place votes of $i$, $\sum f_{i}=n$, $f_{1}\ge f_{2}\ge f_{3}\ge f_{4}$.  For $|O|\ge 2$ an adversary can keep $p_{O}(i)=f_{i}$ for $i\in O$ and can make every voter whose first choice lies outside $O$ rank the outside item above the whole of $O$, so that in the worst case

$p_{O}(i)\ge f_{i},\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i},$

and for a singleton $c_{\{i\}}(j)\le n-f_{i}$.  Hence, up to the usual
adversarial ranking, a set $O$ can be made $>t$-loaded iff
$\min_{i\in O}f_{i}\ge t+1$ and its external cost is $n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i}$.

Put $k=\#\{i:f_{i}\ge t+1\}$.  If $k\ge3$ we can take the three
$t$-large items and the outside cost is $f_{4}\le n/4$; if $k=2$ we can
take the two $t$-large items and the outside cost is $f_{3}+f_{4}\le2t$;
if $k\ge4$ the cost is $0$.  The only obstruction is $k\le1$.

If $k=1$, say $f_{1}\ge t+1$ and $f_{2},f_{3},f_{4}\le t$, then no
$|O|\ge2$ can be $>t$-loaded in the worst case.  The only feasible
choice is the singleton $O=\{1\}$, $p_{O}(1)=n>t$ and

$\max_{j\ne1}c_{j}(\{1\})=n-f_{1}=f_{2}+f_{3}+f_{4}\le3t.$

The bound is attained for $f_{1}=t+1$, $f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=t$,
$n=4t+1$, e.g. $t=20$, $f_{1}=21$, $f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=20$, $n=81$.
On that profile any $O$ with $|O|\ge2$ contains an $i$ with $f_{i}=t< t+1$,
so in the worst ranking $p_{O}(i)=t$.  The best singleton is
$O=\{1\}$ and $n-f_{1}=60$ agents can be made to prefer $2,3$ or $4$
to $1$.  With a Condorcet winner or with $k\ge2$ the cost drops to
$\le2t$ and then to $\le t$.  In particular

$\displaystyle u_{\rm unif}^{\max}= (m-1)t =3t,$

i.e. $u_{\rm unif}=60$ for $t=20$, and $u=3t$ is best possible in the
$n$-free sense.  In the strict $\ge t+1$ counting this is $u=3t$,
$61$ in the $t+1$ notation, the $n-\max f_{i}\le3t$ singleton bound
quoted as $u=(m-1)(t+1)$.

On the conventional normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ the $k\ge3$
case is the one that is normally quoted.  Then $f_{j_{0}}=\min_{i}f_{i}\le
n_{0}/4=t+1$ and with $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$

$c_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=f_{j_{0}}\le t+1,\qquad 
p_{i}(O_{0})\ge\frac{n_{0}-f_{j_{0}}}3\ge t+1,\ i\in O_{0},$

so that

$\min_{|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=\lceil n_{0}/4\rceil=t+1=21,$

i.e. $20$ agents in the strict $>t$ wording.  In the $n_{0}=4t$
loose notation this is the familiar $n/4\approx t$ first-place form
and the $n/2$-pair form

$\min_{|O|=2}\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=n_{0}/2=2(t+1),$

i.e. $2t=40$, $42$ in the $\ge t+1$ convention, attained by the two
opposite linear orders $1\succ2\succ3\succ4$ and $4\succ3\succ2\succ1$
with $n_{0}/2$ voters of each type.  This is the $u\approx2t$,
$u_{0}=t+1\approx20$, bound usually quoted in the literature; the
$60=3t$ singleton bound above is its $n$-free, i.e. $k=1$, uniform
form.  The disagreement in the literature is the $n=4(t+1)$ versus
$n=4t$ versus $n$-free normalisation.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The bound has to be uniform in n. Let $f_i$ be the number of first-place votes for $i$, $f_1\ge f_2\ge f_3\ge f_4$, $\sum f_i=n$, and put $k=\#\{i:f_i\ge t+1\}$ with $t+1=21$.
For $|O|\ge2$ the adversary can keep an agent whose first choice lies in $O$ on that choice and can make every agent whose first choice lies outside $O$ rank the outside item above $O$. In the worst case

\[
\min_{i\in O}{\rm cnt}_O(i)= \min_{i\in O}f_i ,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}{\rm cnt}_{>O}(j)=n-\sum_{i\in O}f_i ,
\]

and for a singleton $O=\{i\}$

\[
{\rm cnt}_O(i)=n,\qquad\max_{j\ne i}{\rm cnt}_{>O}(j)=n-f_i .
\]

Hence a $>t$–supported set with $|O|\ge2$ exists only if $\min_{i\in O}f_i\ge21$. If $k\ge2$ we can take $O$ to be two of the $f_i\ge21$ items and the outside charge is $f_3+f_4\le40$, if $k\ge3$ it is $f_4\le20$, etc.

The difficult case is $k=1$. Then $f_1\ge21$, $f_2,f_3,f_4\le20$. No $O$ with $|O|\ge2$ can be $>t$-loaded because it always contains an item with $f_i\le20<t+1$. The only admissible set in the worst case is the singleton $O=\{1\}$. Then

\[
\max_{j\ne1}c_j(\{1\})=n-f_1=f_2+f_3+f_4\le3\cdot20=60 .
\]

The bound is attained. Take $f_1=21$, $f_2=f_3=f_4=20$, $n=81$, e.g. 21 agents $1\succ2\succ3\succ4$ and 20 agents of each of the three other cyclic orders. Any $O$ with $|O|\ge2$ contains an item with 20 first-place votes, so condition (1) fails, and with $O=\{1\}$ we have ${\rm cnt}_O(1)=81>20$ and $60$ agents can be made to rank $2,3$ or $4$ above $1$. 

The same phenomenon is visible on the $4t$ cycle $f_i\equiv20$, $n=80$. Then $\min\{m_{ij},m_{ji}\}=20<t+1$ for every pair, so no pair and no triple can be $>t$-loaded. The best singleton gives $n-\max f_i=80-20=60$.

If a Condorcet winner $w$ exists then $f_j\le20$ for $j\ne w$ and $n-f_w\le60$; if no Condorcet winner exists then $f_i\le20$ for all $i$, $n\le80$ and $n-\max f_i\le60$. Hence $u=60$ suffices for every profile and $u<60$ is impossible on the $21,20,20,20$ profile. 

The $u\approx2t=40$ statements are the $n$-normalised forms $n\approx4t$ or $n=4(t+1)=84$ where a $t$-loaded triple can be forced and the outside charge can be written as $n/4$ or $n/2$. With $n$ left free the quantifiers ask for a uniform guarantee, which is the singleton first-place guarantee $n-\max f_i\le3t$. For $t=20$ this is the sharp uniform constant $u=60$.

5.text:
For a profile put
$f_{i}=|\{v:i={\rm top}(v)\}|$, $\sum_{i}f_{i}=n$ and
$p_{i}(O)=|\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\}|$, 
$c_{j}(O)=|\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\}|$, $j\notin O$.
In the worst case an adversary can keep

worst case

$$
\min_{i\in O}p_{i}(O)=\min_{i\in O}f_{i},\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i}, \qquad |O|\ge 2,
$$

and for a singleton
$p_{i}(\{i\})=n$ and $\max_{j\ne i}c_{j}(\{i\})=n-f_{i}$.

Put $f_{1}\ge f_{2}\ge f_{3}\ge f_{4}$ and $k=\#\{i:f_{i}\ge t+1\}$.

$$
\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=f_{3}+f_{4}\le2t,
$$

and for $k\ge3$ the outside charge is $\le t$.
The difficult case is $k\le1$.

$$
\max_{j\ne i_{\max}}c_{j}(O)=n-f_{i_{\max}}\le3t .
$$

If $k=1$, say $f_{1}\ge t+1$, $f_{2},f_{3},f_{4}\le t$, no set
$|O|\ge2$ can be $>t$-loaded and the only admissible worst case set is
the singleton $O=\{1\}$.  Then

$$
\max_{j\ne1}c_{j}(\{1\})=n-f_{1}=f_{2}+f_{3}+f_{4}\le3t,
$$

and the bound is attained for the extremal first–place profile

$$
f_{1}=t+1,\qquad f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=t,\qquad n=4t+1,
$$

e.g. $t=20$

$$
f_{1}=21,\;f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=20,\qquad n=81,
$$

on which $O=\{1\}$ is the unique $>t$-loaded set and the adversary can

$$
c_{j}(\{1\})=n-f_{1}=60,\qquad j=2,3,4,
$$

agents prefer any $j\ne1$ to $1$.  The $20\!:\!20\!:\!20\!:\!20$ cyclic

$$
\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)\le (m-1)t,

$$
u^{*}_{\rm uni}=(m-1)t=3t,
$$

c_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=f_{j_{0}}\le n_{0}/4=t+1=21,

9.text:
For a profile put

$f_{i}=|\{v:i={\rm top}(v)\}|$, $\sum_{i}f_{i}=n$, $f_{1}\ge f_{2}\ge f_{3}
\ge f_{4}$ and for $O\ne\varnothing$

$p_{O}(i)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\},\qquad 
c_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}k\;\forall k\in O\},~j\notin O$.
Then $\sum_{i\in O}p_{O}(i)=n-\sum_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)$ and in the
worst adversarial ordering

$p_{O}(i)\ge f_{i},~~|O|\ge2$,  $c_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i}$,
$j\notin O$,

and for a singleton $p_{\{i\}}(i)=n$,
$\max_{j\ne i}c_{j}(\{i\})=n-f_{i}$.  Up to the $+1$ slack a set
$|O|\ge2$ can be made $>t$--loaded iff $\min_{i\in O}f_{i}\ge t+1$ and
its worst external charge is $n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i}$.

Put $k=\#\{i:f_{i}\ge t+1\}$ and $S=\{i:f_{i}\ge t+1\}$.  If $k\ge2$
we can take $O=S$ and

$c(O)=n-\sum_{i\in S}f_{i}=\sum_{i\notin S}f_{i}\le (m-k)t\le2t$,
and if $k\ge3$, $c(O)\le t$.  The only essential case is $k\le1$.

If $k=0$ then $f_{i}\le t$ for every $i$, $n\le mt$, and with
$i_{0}={\rm argmax} f_{i}$,

$p_{\{i_{0}\}}(i_{0})=n>t,\qquad 
\max_{j\ne i_{0}}c_{j}(\{i_{0}\})=n-f_{i_{0}}\le mt-\lceil n/m\rceil
\le (m-1)t$.

If $k=1$, say $f_{1}\ge t+1$, $f_{2},f_{3},f_{4}\le t$, no $|O|\ge2$
can be made $>t$--loaded in the worst case.  The unique admissible
set in the worst case is the singleton $O=\{1\}$ and

$\max_{j\ne1}c_{j}(\{1\})=n-f_{1}=f_{2}+f_{3}+f_{4}\le3t,$

with equality for

$f_{1}=t+1,\;f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=t,\qquad n=4t+1,$

e.g. for $t=20$

$f_{1}=21,\;f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=20,\qquad n=81$,

$O=\{1\}$ is the only $>t$--supported set, $p_{O}(1)=81>20$ and in the
worst ordering $c_{j}(O)=n-f_{1}=60$, $j=2,3,4$.  Up to relabelling this
is the $20\!-\!20\!-\!20\!-\!20$ cyclic profile $n=4t=80$ for which
every pair has $\min\{m_{ij},m_{ji}\}=t$ and the best singleton has
$n-\max f_{i}=3t$.

Hence for every profile there is an $O$ with $p_{O}(i)>t$, $i\in O$, and

$\displaystyle \max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)\le (m-1)t$,

and $(m-1)t$ is best possible in the $n$--free uniform sense.  For
$m=4$

$u_{*}(m,t)=(m-1)t=3t$,

i.e. $u_{*}=60$ for $t=20$.  With the strict $p_{O}(i)\ge t+1$
convention this is $u_{*}=3(t+1)-3=61$, $60$ agents in the loose
$>t$ notation.  The extremal first place profile $21\!-\!20\!-\!20\!-\!20$
shows the bound is tight and is the usual $u=(m-1)t$ singleton
guarantee.

Remark.  On the canonical normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ the
three set $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ with $j_{0}$ a least first place
item can be made $>t$--supported and

$c_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=f_{j_{0}}\le n_{0}/4=t+1$,

$p_{i}(O_{0})\ge (n_{0}-f_{j_{0}})/3\ge t+1$, $i\in O_{0}$.
Hence on the $84$--voter scale the sharp first place form is

$\min_{|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=\lceil n_{0}/4\rceil=t+1=21,$

i.e. $20$ agents in the strict $>t$ wording, and in the usual pair
form $\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=n_{0}/2=2(t+1)$.  This is the familiar

10.text:
For a set $O$ write
$$
p_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\},\qquad 
c_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\},\qquad j\notin O,
$$
and  $f_{i}=\#\{v:i={\rm top}(v)\}$, $\sum_{i}f_{i}=n$,
$f_{1}\ge f_{2}\ge f_{3}\ge f_{4}$.  Up to the worst rank ordering
an adversary can make
$$
p_{i}(O)=f_{i},\qquad i\in O,\qquad 
c_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i},\qquad j\notin O,
$$
for $|O|\ge 2$, and $c_{j}(\{i\})=n-f_{i}$ for a singleton.  In
particular a set $O$ can be made $>t$–loaded in the worst case iff
$\min_{i\in O}f_{i}\ge t+1$ and then
$$
\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i}.
$$
Put $k=\#\{i:f_{i}\ge t+1\}$.
If $k\ge2$ we can take $O$ to be the $k$ large first place items and
$$
\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=\sum_{i>k}f_{i}\le (4-k)t .
$$
The only non trivial regime is $k\le1$.  Then no $O$ with $|O|\ge2$
can be made $>t$–loaded and the only $t$-admissible set which can be
forced in the worst case is a singleton $O=\{i_{0}\}$ with
$f_{i_{0}}=\max_{i}f_{i}$.  For a singleton
$$
p_{i_{0}}(\{i_{0}\})=n>t,\qquad 
\max_{j\ne i_{0}}c_{j}(\{i_{0}\})=n-f_{i_{0}}=f_{2}+f_{3}+f_{4},
$$
so that in the worst case
$$
U(P)=\min_{O}\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=n-\max_{i}f_{i}\le3t .
$$
The bound is attained, e.g. for
$$
f_{1}=t+1,\qquad f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=t,\qquad n=4t+1,
$$
i.e. for $t=20$
$$
f_{1}=21,\;f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=20,\;n=81,
$$
on the four cyclic orders.  On that profile no pair can be made
$>t$–loaded, the unique $t$–admissible set in the worst case is the
singleton $\{1\}$ and the adversary can make
$$
c_{j}(\{1\})=n-f_{1}=60,\qquad j=2,3,4,
$$
agents prefer $j$ to $1$.  With the usual $n=4t$ critical
normalisation this is the familiar $n-\max f_{i}=3n/4=3t$ singleton
guarantee, $3t=60$ agents for $t=20$, i.e. $(m-1)t$ in the loose
$\ge t$ notation and $(m-1)(t+1)=63$ in the strict $\ge t+1$
notation.  Up to the harmless $+1$ this is the $u\approx(m-1)t$
uniform worst case.

In particular on the canonical minimal feasible population
$n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ the three point core can be forced.  Let
$j_{0}$ be a least first place item, $f_{j_{0}}=\min_{i}f_{i}$.
Then
$$
O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\},\qquad 
p_{i}(O_{0})\ge t+1\;(i\in O_{0}),\qquad 
c_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=f_{j_{0}}\le n_{0}/4=t+1,
$$
so that in first place language
$$
\min_{|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=\Big\lceil\frac{n_{0}}4\Big\rceil
=t+1=21,
$$
i.e. $20$ agents in the strict $>t$ wording.  In the usual pair
formulation this is
$$
\min_{|O|=2}\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=\frac{n_{0}}2=2(t+1),
$$
the $2t$ bound $2t=40$ agents, $2(t+1)=42$ in the strict $\ge t+1$
convention, which is the $t+1\approx t$ first place bound quoted in
the literature.  The $60=3t$ singleton value is the $n$-free uniform
supremum; the $21\approx20$, i.e. the $2t\approx40$, value is its

4.text:
Write $f_{i}$ for the number of first place votes of $i$ and put
$f_{1}\ge f_{2}\ge f_{3}\ge f_{4}$, $\sum f_{i}=n$ and for $O\ne\varnothing$

$$
p_{O}(i)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\},\qquad 
c_{O}(j)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}k\;\forall k\in O\},\qquad j\notin O .
$$

Then $\sum_{i\in O}p_{O}(i)=n$ and for $|O|\ge 2$ the adversary can
make

$$
p_{O}(i)=f_{i},\qquad i\in O,\qquad 
c_{O}(j)=n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i},\qquad j\notin O ,
\tag{*}
$$

and for a singleton $p_{\{i\}}(i)=n$ and $c_{\{i\}}(j)=n-f_{i}$.
Hence, up to the usual $+1$ slack, $O$ can be made $t$ -loaded in the
worst case iff $\min_{i\in O}f_{i}\ge t+1$ and its outside charge is

$n-f_{i}$.

Put $k=\#\{i:f_{i}\ge t+1\}$.  If $k\ge 2$ we may take $O$ to be the
$k$ items with $f_{i}\ge t+1$ and then
$\max_{j\notin O}c_{O}(j)=n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i}\le\sum_{i>k}f_{i}\le
