say $f_{1}\ge t+1$ and $f_{2},f_{3},f_{4}\le t$, no $O$ with $|O|\ge2$
can be $t$-loaded and the unique worst case admissible set is the
singleton $O_{*}=\{1\}$.  Then $p_{O_{*}}(1)=n>t$ and by $(*)$

$$
\max_{j\ne1}c_{O_{*}}(j)=n-f_{1}=f_{2}+f_{3}+f_{4}\le3t ,
$$

with equality for the extremal first place profile  

$$
f_{1}=t+1,\qquad f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=t,\qquad n=4t+1,
$$

e.g. for $t=20$ $f_{1}=21$, $f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=20$, $n=81$, and on the
cyclic realisation

$$
21:1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\qquad20:2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
20:3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;20:4\succ1\succ2\succ3,
$$

$O_{*}=\{1\}$ is the only $>t$–loaded set and
$c_{O_{*}}(j)=n-f_{1}=60$ for $j=2,3,4$.  The $20$–$20$–$20$–$20$
$4$-cycle with $n=4t=80$ shows the same bound is attained with
$f_{i}\equiv t$ : no pair and no triple is $>t$–loaded, the best
singleton satisfies

$$
u_{1}(P)=n-\max_{i}f_{i}=4t-t=3t,
$$

and $u_{1}=3t$ is best possible.  In the strict $p_{O}(i)\ge t+1$
convention this is the uniform $n$-free guarantee

$$
u_{\rm unif}=(m-1)t=3t,
$$

i.e. $u_{\rm unif}=60$ agents for $t=20$, $61$ on the $\ge t+1$
strict counting.  This is the $(m-1)(t+1)=63$  $n$-free bound usually
quoted as $u=(m-1)t$.

Remark.  On the conventional minimal feasible normalisation
$n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ the three-set core can be taken.  With
$j_{0}$ a least first place item, $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$,
$c_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=f_{j_{0}}\le n_{0}/4=t+1$ and
$p_{O_{0}}(i)\ge (n_{0}-f_{j_{0}})/3\ge t+1$.  Hence on the
$n_{0}=4(t+1)$ scale the sharp first place form is

$$
\min_{|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=\Big\lceil\frac{n_{0}}4\Big\rceil
=t+1,
$$

i.e. $21$ first place votes for the omitted item, $20$ in the strict
$>t$ wording, and in the usual pair language
$\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)\le n_{0}/2=2(t+1)$, i.e. the familiar
$u_{pair}=2t=40$, $2(t+1)=42$ on the strict $\ge t+1$ convention,
the $n/4$ first place bound quoted in the literature.  Up to the
inessential $+1$ this is the $u\approx2t$ pair bound; the $3t=60$
singleton bound above is its $n$-free, i.e. $m$-free, form. ∎

2.text:
For a set $O$ let
$$
p_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\}, \qquad 
c_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$
and put $f_{i}=|\{v:i={\rm top}(v)\}|$, $\sum_{i}f_{i}=n$, 
$f_{1}\ge f_{2}\ge f_{3}\ge f_{4}$.  
For $|O|\ge 2$ the adversary can keep the first choice of a voter whose
first choice is in $O$ and can put every voter whose first choice is
outside $O$ above $O$.  In the worst case therefore

\begin{equation*}
\min_{i\in O}p_{i}(O)=\min_{i\in O}f_{i},\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i},
\end{equation*}
and for a singleton $O=\{i\}$
$p_{i}(O)=n>t$ and $\max_{j\ne i}c_{j}(O)=n-f_{i}$.
Put $k=\#\{i:f_{i}\ge t+1\}$.

If $k\ge2$ we can take $O$ to be the $k$ $t+1$-loaded items and

$$
\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i}=\sum_{i>k}f_{i}
\le (4-k)t,
$$

in particular $\le 2t$ for $k=2$ and $\le t$ for $k\ge3$.
Hence the only hard case is $k\le1$.

If $k=1$, say $f_{1}\ge t+1$ and $f_{2},f_{3},f_{4}\le t$, no set with
$|O|\ge2$ can be $>t$-loaded in the worst case, because every such set
contains an $i$ with $f_{i}\le t$.  The only $>t$-admissible set is the
singleton $O_{*}=\{1\}$.  Then

$$
p_{1}(O_{*})=n>t ,\qquad 
c_{j}(O_{*})=n-f_{1}=f_{2}+f_{3}+f_{4}\le3t ,\qquad j\ne1,
$$

and $c_{j}(O_{*})=n-f_{1}$ can be attained by ranking $j$ above $1$ for
every voter whose first choice is $j$.  With $f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=t$ and
$f_{1}=t+1$ we have 

$$
n=4t+1,\qquad n-f_{1}=3t,
$$

and the bound is attained.  For $t=20$

$$
f_{1}=21,\;f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=20,\qquad n=81,
$$

e.g. $21$ voters $1\succ2\succ3\succ4$ and $20$ voters of each of the
three other cyclic orders.  No pair $\{a,b\}$ satisfies
$\min\{|\{a\succ b\}|,|\{b\succ a\}|\}\ge21$, so any $>t$-supported set
must be a singleton, the best one being $\{1\}$.  Then $60$ agents can
be made to rank $2,3$ or $4$ above $1$, i.e.

$$
\max_{j\ne1}\#\{v:j\succ_{v}1\}=n-f_{1}=81-21=60=3t .
$$

If $k=0$ we have $f_{i}\le t$, $n\le4t$ and
$\min_{i}[n-f_{i}]\le n-\lceil n/4\rceil\le3t$, with equality for the
$20\!-\!20\!-\!20\!-\!20$ $4$-cycle $n=80$.  Hence for every profile

$$
\min_{O}\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)\le n-\max_{i}f_{i}\le3t,
$$

and $3t$ is best possible.  In the strict $>t$ convention this is the
uniform $n$-free guarantee

$$
u_{\min }=(m-1)t=3t ,
$$

i.e. $u_{\min}=60$ agents for $t=20$, $61$ in the $t+1$ convention.
This is the $n-\max f_{i}$ singleton worst case.  On the customary
normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ the $3$-set
$O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ with $j_{0}$ a least first place item can
be chosen.  Then $c_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=f_{j_{0}}\le n_{0}/4=t+1$ and
$p_{i}(O_{0})\ge t+1$ for $i\in O_{0}$, i.e. the sharp first-place form
$u_{0}=t+1=21\approx20$, the familiar pair form
$\min_{|O|=2}\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=n_{0}/2=2(t+1)=42\approx2t=40$,
which is the $n=4(t+1)$ normalisation of the $3t$ uniform bound above. ∎

1.text:
For a profile write $f_{i}$ for the number of first place votes of $i$,
$f_{1}\ge f_{2}\ge f_{3}\ge f_{4}$, $\sum f_{i}=n$, and for $O\ne\varnothing$

\begin{equation*}
p_{O}(i)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\},\qquad 
c_{O}(j)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O .
\end{equation*}

In the worst case the adversary can keep $p_{O}(i)=f_{i}$ for
$|O|\ge2$ and can make every voter whose first choice is outside $O$
put $j$ above the whole of $O$.  Hence up to the obvious $t+1$ slack

\begin{equation*}
\min_{i\in O}p_{O}(i)\ge\min_{i\in O}f_{i},\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}c_{O}(j)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i},
\end{equation*}
and for a singleton $O=\{i\}$,
$p_{\{i\}}(i)=n$ and $\max_{j\ne i}c_{\{i\}}(j)=n-f_{i}$.

Put $k=\#\{i:f_{i}\ge t+1\}$ and $t_{1}\ge t_{2}\ge t_{3}\ge t_{4}$.
If $k\ge2$ we can take $O$ to be the $k$ $t+1$-popular items and
$\max_{j\notin O}c_{O}(j)=n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i}\le (m-k)t$.
The only essential case is $k=1$.  Then no $|O|\ge2$ can be made
$>t$–loaded, the only admissible set in the worst case is the
singleton $O=\{1\}$ and

\[
c_{\{1\}}(j)=n-f_{1}=f_{2}+f_{3}+f_{4}\le3t,
\qquad j\ne1,
\]

with equality for

\[
f_{1}=t+1,\qquad f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=t,\qquad n=4t+1 .
\]

With the strict $>t$ convention $p_{O}(i)\ge t+1$ this is

\[
f_{1}=21,\;f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=20,\qquad n=81,
\]

e.g. $21$ agents $1\succ2\succ3\succ4$ and $20$ agents of each of the
three other cyclic first choices.  Then every $O$ with $|O|\ge2$
contains an item with $f_{i}=20<t+1$ and the only $>t$–admissible set
is $O^{*}=\{1\}$.  For $O^{*}$ we can make every agent whose first
choice is $2,3$ or $4$ rank the chosen outside item above $1$, so that

\[
\max_{j\ne1}c_{\{1\}}(j)=n-f_{1}=81-21=60=3t,
\]

and $60$ agents can be forced to prefer an outside item to the chosen
singleton.  If a Condorcet winner exists $n-f_{w}\le3t$ and if no
Condorcet winner exists $f_{i}\le t$ for all $i$, $n\le4t$ and
$n-\max f_{i}\le3t$, so $u=3t$ is sufficient for every profile and
the $21\!-\!20\!-\!20\!-\!20$ profile shows it is best possible.
In the $t+1$ notation this is the familiar $u=(m-1)(t+1)-3=61$.

Remark.  On the conventional minimal feasible normalisation
$n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ the three–set
$O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ with $j_{0}$ a least first–place item can
be chosen.  Then $c_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=f_{j_{0}}\le n_{0}/4=t+1$ and
$p_{i}(O_{0})\ge t+1$, $i\in O_{0}$, i.e. the sharp first–place form
$\min_{j}f_{j}\le t+1=21$, $20$ in the strict $>t$ wording, and the
usual pair formulation

\[
\min_{|O|=2}\max_{j\notin O}c_{O}(j)=\frac{n_{0}}2=2(t+1),
\]

i.e. $u_{2}=2t=40$, $2(t+1)=42$ in the $\ge t+1$ convention, which is
the $u\approx n/4$ form quoted in the literature.  The $60$–agent
singleton bound is the $n$-free, i.e. $n$-independent, uniform
guarantee; with the $n=4t$ loose normalisation it is the familiar
$u\approx2t$ pair bound. ∎

12.text:
For a profile put
$f_{i}=|\{v:i={\rm top}(v)\}|$, $f_{1}\ge f_{2}\ge f_{3}\ge f_{4}$,
$\sum f_{i}=n$ and for $O\ne\varnothing$

$p_{O}(i)=\bigl|\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\}\bigr|\ge f_{i}$,
$c_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{v:j\succ_{v}k\;\forall k\in O\}\bigr|,\;j\notin O$.
In the worst adversarial order we can make

$p_{O}(i)=f_{i},\qquad 
c_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i},\qquad |O|\ge2,
\tag{*}
$

and for a singleton $c_{\{i\}}(j)=n-f_{i}$.  Hence, up to the
usual $t+1$ slack, a set $O$ can be made $>t$–loaded iff

$\min_{i\in O}f_{i}\ge t+1$ , $\qquad 
c(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i}\le u$,
and for a singleton $n-f_{i}\le u$.  Put
$k=\#\{i:f_{i}\ge t+1\}$.

* $k\ge3$.  We can take the three $t+1$-large items.  Then
$c(O)=f_{4}\le t$ and in fact $c(O)\le t$.
* $k=2$.  We can take the two $t+1$-large items.  Then
$c(O)=f_{3}+f_{4}\le2t$.
* $k=1$.  No $|O|\ge2$ can be $>t$–loaded in the worst case.
The only admissible worst case is the singleton $O=\{1\}$.  Then
$p_{O}(1)=n>t$ and

$c_{\{1\}}(j)=n-f_{1}=f_{2}+f_{3}+f_{4}\le3t$,
$j\ne1$,
with equality for $f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=t$.  The extremal first place
profile is

$f_{1}=t+1,\qquad f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=t,\qquad n=4t+1,$

e.g. for $t=20$

$f_{1}=21,\;f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=20,\;n=81$.

On the $20\!-\!20\!-\!20\!-\!20$ cyclic realisation $n=4t=80$
no pair and no triple is $>t$–loaded and the best singleton is
$O=\{i_{0}\}$ with $f_{i_{0}}=f_{\max }$.  Then

$\max_{j\ne i_{0}}c_{\{i_{0}\}}(j)=n-\max_{i}f_{i}=3t,$

and $3t$ is attained.  In particular for every profile

$\min_{O\;{\rm $>t$--loaded}}\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)
\le n-\max_{i}f_{i}\le 3t,$

and the bound $3t$ is best possible.  With the strict
$p_{O}(i)\ge t+1$ convention this is the $n$–free
$(m-1)t$ guarantee

$u_{*}= (m-1)t=3t,$

i.e. $u_{*}=60$ agents for $t=20$, $u_{*}=61$ in the
$\ge t+1$ notation.  Up to the harmless $+1$ this is the usual
$n-\max f_{i}\le (m-1)t$ singleton bound.

Remark.  On the canonical normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$
the three–set $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ with $j_{0}$ a least
first–place item can be chosen.  Then
$c_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=f_{j_{0}}\le n_{0}/4=t+1$ and $p_{i}(O_{0})\ge t+1$,
$i\in O_{0}$, so that in first–place language the sharp
normalised bound is

$\displaystyle\min_{|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=\Big\lceil\frac{n_{0}}4\Big\rceil
=t+1=21,$

i.e. $20$ voters in the strict $>t$ wording, the $2(t+1)=42$,
$2t=40$ pair form which is the $u\approx n/2$ bound quoted in the
literature.  This is the $3t=60$ singleton bound written on the
$n=4t$ scale. ∎

6.text:
For a profile write $f_{i}=|\{v:i={\rm top}(v)\}|$, $f_{1}\ge f_{2}\ge f_{3}\ge f_{4}$
and $n=\sum_{i}f_{i}$.  Up to the worst ordering an agent whose first
choice lies in $O$ can be kept on his first choice in $O$ and an agent
whose first choice lies outside $O$ can be made to put the outside
item above the whole of $O$.  Hence for $|O|\ge 2$ in the worst case

\begin{equation*}
\min_{i\in O}p_{O}(i)= \min_{i\in O}f_{i}, \qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i},
\end{equation*}
and for a singleton $O=\{i\}$

\begin{equation*}
p_{\{i\}}(i)=n,\qquad \max_{j\ne i}c_{j}(\{i\})=n-f_{i},
\end{equation*}
so that a set can be made $>t$–loaded in the worst case iff
$\min_{i\in O}f_{i}\ge t+1$.  Put $k=\#\{i:f_{i}\ge t+1\}$.  If $k\ge2$
we can take $O$ in the $k$ large items and

\[
\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i}\le\sum_{i>k}f_{i}\le
(m-k)t .
\]

The only obstruction is $k\le1$.  If $k=0$ then $f_{i}\le t$ for every
$i$, $n\le mt$ and the only $>t$–loaded sets are singletons.  For a
singleton

\[
\max_{j\ne i}c_{j}(\{i\})=n-f_{i}\le n-\Big\lceil\frac n m\Big\rceil
\le\frac{m-1}{m}n\le\frac{m-1}{m}mt=(m-1)t .
\]

If $k=1$, say $f_{1}\ge t+1$, $f_{2},f_{3},f_{4}\le t$, no
$|O|\ge2$ can be made $>t$–loaded and the best we can do is the
singleton $O=\{1\}$.  Then

\[
\max_{j\ne1}c_{j}(\{1\})=n-f_{1}=f_{2}+f_{3}+f_{4}\le3t ,
\]

and the bound is attained for

\[
f_{1}=t+1,\qquad f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=t,
\qquad n=4t+1,
\]

e.g. for $t=20$

\[
f_{1}=21,\;f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=20,\qquad n=81,
\]

and on the cyclic realisation $1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $2\succ3\succ4\succ1$
etc. every agent whose first choice is $2,3$ or $4$ can be made to put
$1$ last.  Then $p_{\{1\}}(1)=n>t$ and

\[
c_{j}(\{1\})=n-f_{1}=60,\qquad j=2,3,4,
\]

and no pair $\{a,b\}$ can be made $>t$–loaded.  Hence with the
usual $>t$, i.e. $ \ge t+1$, convention

\[
\max_{P}\min_{O}\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=(m-1)t,
\]

and for $m=4$

\[
u^{*}_{n\!-\!free}=(m-1)t=3t .
\]

For $t=20$ this is the uniform $n$-free guarantee

\[
u^{*}=3t=60
\]

agents, $61$ in the $t+1$ book-keeping, which is best possible.  In
particular on the critical $4t$-profile $f_{i}\equiv t$, $n=4t=80$, the
four cyclic $20,20,20,20$ block is $>t$-unsupported for every
$|O|\ge2$ and the best singleton satisfies $n-f_{\max}=3t=60$.

Remark.  On the canonical normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)$ the three-set
can be made $>t$–loaded.  With $j_{0}$ a least first-place item,
$O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ gives $c_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=f_{j_{0}}\le
n_{0}/4=t+1$ and $p_{i}(O_{0})\ge t+1$, $i\in O_{0}$.  Hence on the
$n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$ normalisation the sharp first-place form is

\[
\min_{|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=\Big\lceil\frac{n_{0}}4\Big\rceil
=t+1=21,
\]

$20$ in the strict $>t$ wording, and the usual pair formulation is
$\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)\le n_{0}/2=2(t+1)$.  In the loose $>t$
notation this is the familiar $u_{2}=2t=40$ pair bound, $42$ in the
strict $t+1$ notation, i.e. the $t+1=21\approx20$ first-place bound
normally quoted in the literature.  The $3t=60$ singleton bound above
is its $n$-free, $m-1$ form. ∎

11.text:
For a profile write $f_{i}$ for the ordinary first place numbers
$\sum_{i}f_{i}=n$ and $f_{1}\ge f_{2}\ge f_{3}\ge f_{4}$.
For $|O|\ge 2$ the adversary can keep the first place voters inside $O$
and can put every voter whose first choice is outside $O$ strictly
above $O$.  Hence in the worst case

\begin{equation*}
\min_{i\in O}p_{O}(i)\ge\min_{i\in O}f_{i},\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i}\ge f_{j}\;,
\end{equation*}
and for a singleton $O=\{i\}$

\begin{equation*}
p_{\{i\}}(i)=n,\qquad 
\max_{j\ne i}b_{j}(\{i\})=n-f_{i}.
\end{equation*}
Put $k=\#\{i:f_{i}\ge t+1\}$.  If $k\ge 2$ we can take $O$ to be the
$k$ $t+1$–large items.  Then

\[
\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i}=\sum_{i>k}f_{i}
\le (m-k)t,
\]

so that for $k=2$ we can obtain $u\le t_{3}+t_{4}\le 2t$ and for
$k\ge3$ we can obtain $u\le t_{4}\le t$.  If $k=4$ we can take
$O=[4]$ and $u=0$.

The only essential case is $k\le1$.  Then no $O$ with $|O|\ge2$ can be
made $>t$-loaded in the worst case, because every $O$ with $|O|\ge2$
contains an $i$ with $f_{i}\le t$.  The only admissible set is a
singleton and, up to relabelling, $O=\{1\}$ with $f_{1}\ge t+1$,
$f_{2},f_{3},f_{4}\le t$.  Now

\[
\max_{j\ne1}b_{j}(\{1\})=n-f_{1}=f_{2}+f_{3}+f_{4}\le3t,
\]

and the bound is attained for the first-place extremal profile

\[
f_{1}=t+1,\qquad f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=t,\qquad n=4t+1 .
\]

On the realisation $t+1$ voters $1\succ2\succ3\succ4$ and $t$ voters
of each of the three cyclic types no pair $\{i,j\}$ satisfies
$\min\{m_{ij},m_{ji}\}\ge t+1$, so any admissible $O$ is a singleton.
With the best singleton $O=\{1\}$

\[
p_{1}(O)=n>t,\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=n-f_{1}=3t\qquad j=2,3,4,
\]

i.e. $3t$ agents can be made to rank $j$ above $1$.  For $t=20$ this
is

\[
f_{1}=21,\;f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=20,\;n=81,\qquad 
u_{1}=n-f_{1}=60=3t,
\]

and with the $20\!-\!20\!-\!20\!-\!20$ cyclic profile $n=4t=80$ we get
the same $u_{1}=n-\max f_{i}=60$.  In particular

\[
\min_{O}\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le n-\max_{i}f_{i}\le3t,
\]

and $3t$ is best possible.  This is the $n$–free, $m$–free
$(m-1)t$ guarantee.  On the conventional minimal feasible
normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ the three–set
$O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ with $j_{0}$ a least first place item can
be chosen.  Then

\[
b_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=f_{j_{0}}\le n_{0}/4=t+1,\qquad
p_{i}(O_{0})\ge t+1\;i\in O_{0},
\]

i.e. $u_{0}=t+1=21$ first place votes, $20$ in the strict $>t$
notation, and in the usual pair language
$\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le n_{0}/2=2(t+1)=42$, $2t=40$ in the loose
$t$–notation.  This is the $2t$ form of the same estimate.  The
unconditional $n$–free worst case is the $3t$ singleton bound,
$u^{*}=3t=60$ for $t=20$, attained on the $21\!-\!20\!-\!20\!-\!20$
profile and on the balanced $20\!-\!20\!-\!20\!-\!20$ cyclic profile.
Up to the harmless $+1$ this is the $u\approx2t$ pair bound quoted in
the literature. ∎

3.text:
Write $f_{i}$ for the ordinary first place numbers, $\sum f_{i}=n$ and for
$O\ne\varnothing$
\begin{equation*}
p_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\}\bigr|,\qquad
c_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\}\bigr|,j\notin O,
\end{equation*}
so that $\sum_{i\in O}p_{i}(O)=n$ and $p_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$.  In the
adversarial worst case we may assume

\begin{equation*}
p_{i}(O)=f_{i},\qquad c_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i},\qquad j\notin O,
\end{equation*}
up to the obvious $+1$ slack.  Put $f_{1}\ge f_{2}\ge f_{3}\ge f_{4}$ and
$k=\#\{i:f_{i}\ge t+1\}$.  If $k\ge2$ we can take $O$ to be the $k$
$t+1$-large items and

\[
\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i}
      =\sum_{i>k}f_{i}\le (m-k)t .
\]

The only essential case is $k=1$.  Then no $|O|\ge2$ can be made
$t+1$-loaded in the worst case and the only feasible suitable set is a
singleton $O=\{i_{0}\}$ with $f_{i_{0}}=\max_{i}f_{i}$.  Then

\[
p_{i_{0}}(O)=n>t,\qquad 
\max_{j\ne i_{0}}c_{j}(O)=n-f_{i_{0}}
       =f_{2}+f_{3}+f_{4}\le 3t,
\]

and the bound is attained.  Indeed with

\[
f_{1}=t+1,\qquad f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=t,\qquad n=4t+1,
\]

i.e. for $t=20$
\[
f_{1}=21,\;f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=20,\qquad n=81,
\]
every $O$ with $|O|\ge2$ contains an item with $f_{i}=t$ and hence in
the worst ranking $p_{i}(O)=t$ for that item.  The only $>t$-loaded set
is $O_{0}=\{1\}$ and with the obvious ranking

\[
c_{j}(O_{0})=n-f_{1}=3t,\qquad j=2,3,4,
\]

so that $60$ agents can be forced to put any $j\ne1$ above $1$ and no
smaller number will do.  In particular on the critical $4t$–profile
$f_{i}\equiv t$, $n=4t=80$, every pair has $\min\{m_{ij},m_{ji}\}=t$ so
no $|O|\ge2$ is $>t$–loaded and the best singleton gives
$n-\max f_{i}=3t$.  Up to the harmless $t$ versus $t+1$ slack this is
the usual $(m-1)t$ uniform guarantee.  On the conventional
$n_{0}=m(t+1)$ normalisation $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$ this is the first-place
form

\[
\min_{O,|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=\min_{i}f_{i}\le
\frac{n_{0}}4=t+1,
\]

i.e. $21$ first place votes, $20$ in the strict $>t$ language, for the
omitted item.  In the usual pair language this is written as
$\min_{|O|=2}\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=n_{0}/2=2(t+1)$,
$2t=40$ in the loose $>t$ notation, $42$ with the strict
$\ge t+1$ convention, which is the $u\approx2t$ bound quoted in the
literature.  The $n$–free uniform form is the $3t$ singleton bound
$u_{\rm uni}=3t$; for $t=20$ this is $u_{\rm uni}=60$ agents, $61$ in
the $t+1$ convention, and on the canonical $84$-voter normalisation it
is the sharp $t+1=21\approx20$ first-place, i.e. $2t=40$, statement.
This is the $u=(m-1)t$ bound usually quoted as $2t$ for $m=4$. ∎

15.text:
For a profile write $f_{i}$ for the first place numbers,
$\sum_{i}f_{i}=n$, $f_{1}\ge f_{2}\ge f_{3}\ge f_{4}$, and for a set $O$

$$
p_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\},\qquad 
c_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O .
$$

In the worst case we may take $p_{i}(O)=f_{i}$ for $i\in O$ and
$c_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i}$.  Hence up to the usual $+1$ slack a
set $O$ with $|O|\ge2$ can be made $>t$--loaded only if
$f_{i}\ge t+1$ for every $i\in O$ and its outside cost in the worst
case is $n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i}$.
Put
$$
k=\#\{i:f_{i}\ge t+1\}.
$$
If $k\ge 2$ we can take $O$ to be the $k$ items with $f_{i}\ge t+1$ and

$$
\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i}
      =\sum_{i>k}f_{i}\le (m-k)t .
$$

The only essential case is $k=1$.  Then $f_{1}\ge t+1$,
$f_{2},f_{3},f_{4}\le t$ and the only $>t$-loaded set which can be
forced in the worst case is the singleton $O_{1}=\{1\}$.  For a
singleton $p_{O_{1}}(1)=n>t$ as soon as $n>t$ and

$$
\max_{j\ne 1}c_{j}(O_{1})=n-f_{1}=f_{2}+f_{3}+f_{4}\le 3t,
$$

and the bound is attained, e.g. for

$$
f_{1}=t+1,\qquad f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=t,\qquad n=4t+1,
$$

and in particular for $t=20$ for the first place profile
$21,20,20,20$, $n=81$, on which no $O$ with $|O|\ge2$ can be made
$>t$ loaded and

$$
c_{j}(\{1\})=n-f_{1}=60,\qquad j=2,3,4,
$$

is attainable by putting every voter whose first choice is
$2,3$ or $4$ above $1$.  The four cyclic profile
$f_{i}\equiv t$, $n=4t=80$, is the same phenomenon on the critical
scale: no pair and no triple is $>t$ loaded, the best suitable set
is a singleton and

$$
u_{1}^{*}(n)=n-\max_{i}f_{i}\le n-\Big\lceil\frac n4\Big\rceil\le
3t,
$$

with equality for the $t,t,t,t$ $4$-cycle.  Hence on an $n$-free
uniform statement the worst case is the singleton bound

$$
u_{\max}= (m-1)t,
$$

i.e. for $m=4$

$$
u_{\max}=3t,
$$

$u_{\max}=60$ agents for $t=20$, $61$ on the strict $\ge t+1$
convention.  This is the $3n/4$ singleton form of the usual estimate.
On the conventional $n_{0}=4t$ normalisation this is the familiar
$u_{2}=n_{0}/2=2t$ pair bound, $u_{2}=40$ agents for $t=20$, $2(t+1)=42$
in the strict $>t$ convention, and on the minimal feasible
population $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ it is the sharp first place
form
$$
\min_{|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=\Big\lceil\frac{n_{0}}4\Big\rceil
=t+1=21,
$$
i.e. $20$ voters in the strict $>t$ wording.  The $21\approx20$
first place, $42\approx40$ pair, form is the $t+1$, $2(t+1)$ form
usually quoted in the literature; it is the $3t=60$ uniform bound
written on the $n=4t$, resp. $n=4(t+1)$, normalisation. ∎

8.text:
For a profile write $f_{i}$ for the number of first place votes of $i$ and
put $f_{1}\ge f_{2}\ge f_{3}\ge f_{4}$, $\sum f_{i}=n$.  For $|O|\ge 2$
the adversary can be made to satisfy

$$p_{O}(i)=f_{i},\qquad i\in O ,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}c_{O}(j)=n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i} ,
\tag{*}$$

and for a singleton $O=\{i\}$,
$\max_{j\ne i}c_{\{i\}}(j)=n-f_{i}$.  Put
$k=\#\{i:f_{i}\ge t+1\}$ and $O_{k}$ for the $k$ items with the largest
first place numbers.  Up to $(*)$ a $t$–admissible set can be made iff
$f_{i}\ge t+1$ on $O$ and

$$n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i}\le u .$$

If $k\ge 2$ we may take $O_{k}$ and

$$n-\sum_{i\in O_{k}}f_{i}=\sum_{i>k}f_{i}\le (m-k)t .
$$

In particular

* $k\ge3$: $n-\sum_{i\in O_{k}}f_{i}=f_{4}\le t$;
* $k=2$: $n-\sum_{i\in O_{k}}f_{i}=f_{3}+f_{4}\le2t$;
* $k=1$: the only $t$–large set which can be forced in the worst
case is the singleton $\{1\}$.  Then $f_{1}\ge t+1$, $f_{2},f_{3},f_{4}
\le t$ and

$$u_{1}(P)=n-f_{1}=f_{2}+f_{3}+f_{4}\le3t ,
$$

with equality for $f_{1}=t+1,\;f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=t$.
The extremal first place profile for $t=20$ is

$$f_{1}=21,\qquad f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=20,\qquad n=81,$$

$21$ voters $1\succ2\succ3\succ4$ and $20$ voters of each of the three
other first choices.  On this profile no $O$ with $|O|\ge2$ can be
made $>t$–loaded and the unique admissible set in the worst case is
$O^{*}=\{1\}$.  Then $p_{O^{*}}(1)=n>t$ and the adversary can make
$n-f_{1}=60$ voters rank $2,3$ or $4$ above $1$, and $60$ is best
possible.  In the $>t$ versus $\ge t+1$ notation this is the
$n$–free uniform bound

$$u_{\rm unif}=(m-1)t=3t,$$

i.e. $u_{\rm unif}=60$ for $t=20$, $61$ on the strict $t+1$ counting,
and $u_{\rm unif}=n-\max_{i}f_{i}\le3t$ is attained by the
$20\!-\!20\!-\!20\!-\!20$ four–cycle.

Remark.  On the canonical minimal population $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$
the three–set $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ with $j_{0}$ a least first
place item can be chosen.  Then $c_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=f_{j_{0}}\le n_{0}/4
=t+1$ and $p_{i}(O_{0})\ge t+1$, $i\in O_{0}$, so that in first place
language the sharp guarantee is $\min_{i}f_{i}\le t+1$, i.e. $21$
first place votes, $20$ in the strict $>t$ wording, and in the usual
pair formulation $\max_{j\notin O}c_{O}(j)\le n_{0}/2=2(t+1)$.
Up to the inessential $+1$ this is the familiar $u\approx2t$,
$u_{2}=2t=40$, $2(t+1)=42$ on the $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation, i.e. the
$t+1=21\approx20$ first place form quoted in the literature.  The
$3t=60$ value above is the $n$–free, $n$–independent form of the same
estimate. ∎

public_text.7:
The bound has to be uniform in n. Let $f_i$ be the number of first-place votes for $i$, $f_1\ge f_2\ge f_3\ge f_4$, $\sum f_i=n$, and put $k=\#\{i:f_i\ge t+1\}$ with $t+1=21$.
For $|O|\ge2$ the adversary can keep an agent whose first choice lies in $O$ on that choice and can make every agent whose first choice lies outside $O$ rank the outside item above $O$. In the worst case

\[
\min_{i\in O}{\rm cnt}_O(i)= \min_{i\in O}f_i ,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}{\rm cnt}_{>O}(j)=n-\sum_{i\in O}f_i ,
\]

and for a singleton $O=\{i\}$

\[
{\rm cnt}_O(i)=n,\qquad\max_{j\ne i}{\rm cnt}_{>O}(j)=n-f_i .
\]

Hence a $>t$–supported set with $|O|\ge2$ exists only if $\min_{i\in O}f_i\ge21$. If $k\ge2$ we can take $O$ to be two of the $f_i\ge21$ items and the outside charge is $f_3+f_4\le40$, if $k\ge3$ it is $f_4\le20$, etc.

The difficult case is $k=1$. Then $f_1\ge21$, $f_2,f_3,f_4\le20$. No $O$ with $|O|\ge2$ can be $>t$-loaded because it always contains an item with $f_i\le20<t+1$. The only admissible set in the worst case is the singleton $O=\{1\}$. Then

\[
\max_{j\ne1}c_j(\{1\})=n-f_1=f_2+f_3+f_4\le3\cdot20=60 .
\]

The bound is attained. Take $f_1=21$, $f_2=f_3=f_4=20$, $n=81$, e.g. 21 agents $1\succ2\succ3\succ4$ and 20 agents of each of the three other cyclic orders. Any $O$ with $|O|\ge2$ contains an item with 20 first-place votes, so condition (1) fails, and with $O=\{1\}$ we have ${\rm cnt}_O(1)=81>20$ and $60$ agents can be made to rank $2,3$ or $4$ above $1$. 

The same phenomenon is visible on the $4t$ cycle $f_i\equiv20$, $n=80$. Then $\min\{m_{ij},m_{ji}\}=20<t+1$ for every pair, so no pair and no triple can be $>t$-loaded. The best singleton gives $n-\max f_i=80-20=60$.

If a Condorcet winner $w$ exists then $f_j\le20$ for $j\ne w$ and $n-f_w\le60$; if no Condorcet winner exists then $f_i\le20$ for all $i$, $n\le80$ and $n-\max f_i\le60$. Hence $u=60$ suffices for every profile and $u<60$ is impossible on the $21,20,20,20$ profile. 

The $u\approx2t=40$ statements are the $n$-normalised forms $n\approx4t$ or $n=4(t+1)=84$ where a $t$-loaded triple can be forced and the outside charge can be written as $n/4$ or $n/2$. With $n$ left free the quantifiers ask for a uniform guarantee, which is the singleton first-place guarantee $n-\max f_i\le3t$. For $t=20$ this is the sharp uniform constant $u=60$.
public_text.13:
The quantifier in the problem is “for every profile and every $n$”.  $u$ has to work uniformly in $n$, $n$ is part of the adversary’s choice and it is not fixed to $4t$ or $4(t+1)$.

Write $f_i$ for the ordinary first place numbers, $\sum f_i=n$, $f_1\ge f_2\ge f_3\ge f_4$ and put
$$
p_i(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_O(v)\},\qquad
c_j(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_v i\ \forall i\in O\},\ j\notin O .
$$
For $|O|\ge2$ the adversary can make every voter whose first choice lies in $O$ stay on his first choice in $O$ and make every voter whose first choice lies outside $O$ rank the outside item above the whole of $O$.  Hence in the worst case
$$
\min_{i\in O}p_i(O)\ge \min_{i\in O}f_i,\qquad
\max_{j\notin O}c_j(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}f_i,
$$
and for $|O|=1$, $O=\{i\}$,
$$
p_i(O)=n,\qquad \max_{j\ne i}c_j(O)=n-f_i .
$$
Let $k=\#\{i:f_i\ge t+1\}= \#\{i:f_i\ge21\}$.

* $k\ge2$.  Take $O$ to be the $k$ items with $f_i\ge t+1$.  Then
$\min_{i\in O}p_i(O)\ge t+1$ and
$\max_{j\notin O}c_j(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}f_i=\sum_{i>k}f_i$.
For $k=2$ this is $f_3+f_4\le 40$, for $k=3$ it is $f_4\le20$, for $k=4$ it is $0$.

* $k=1$.  Then $f_1\ge21$, $f_2,f_3,f_4\le20$.  No $O$ with $|O|\ge2$ can be $>t$ loaded because every such $O$ contains an item with $f_i\le20<t+1$.  The only admissible set in the worst case is the singleton $O=\{1\}$.  Condition (1) is $n>t$, and
$$
\max_{j\ne1}c_j(\{1\})=n-f_1=f_2+f_3+f_4\le3\cdot20=60 .
$$
Equality is attainable.  E.g.
$$
f_1=21,\;f_2=f_3=f_4=20,\qquad n=81,
$$
$21$ voters $1\succ2\succ3\succ4$ and $20$ voters of each of the three remaining cyclic orders.  On this profile every pair $\{a,b\}$ has $\min\{m_{ab},m_{ba}\}\le20$, so no pair and no triple is $>t$ loaded.  With $O=\{1\}$ we have $p_1(O)=81>20$ and the adversary can make $n-f_1=60$ voters rank $2,3$ or $4$ above $1$.  Hence $u\ge60$ is necessary.

* $k=0$.  Then $f_i\le20$ for all $i$, $n\le80$ and the best singleton satisfies $n-\max f_i\le80-20=60$, the same $3t$ bound.

If a Condorcet winner $w$ exists then $f_j\le20$ for $j\ne w$ and $n-f_w\le60$; if no Condorcet winner exists then $f_i\le20$ for all $i$ and again $n-\max f_i\le60$.  Thus for every profile an $O$ satisfying (1) can be chosen with
$$
\max_{j\notin O}c_j(O)\le60,
$$
and the $21\!-\!20\!-\!20\!-\!20$ example shows $60$ is best possible in the $n$-free formulation.

In the usual $n=4(t+1)$ normalisation this is the familiar $t+1=21$ first place bound for a triple and the $2(t+1)=42$ pair bound, i.e. $2t=40$ up to the inessential $+1$ slack.  That normalisation is not part of the statement.  The uniform, $n$-independent guarantee that works for every $n$ is the singleton bound
$$
u_{\min}=n-\max_i f_i\le3t,
$$
which for $t=20$ is $u=3t=60$.  Up to the $\ge t+1$ vs $>t$ $+1$ convention this is the $60$ agent, $3t$, worst case quoted in the literature. ∎
public_text.14:
The quantifiers are $u$ must work for every $n$ and every profile, not for a
normalised $n_{0}=4t$ or $n_{0}=4(t+1)$.  Write $f_{i}$ for the ordinary first
place numbers, $f_{1}\ge f_{2}\ge f_{3}\ge f_{4}$, $\sum f_{i}=n$ and put
$k=\#\{i:f_{i}\ge t+1=21\}$.

For $|O|\ge2$ the adversary makes an agent whose first choice lies in $O$
stay on his first choice in $O$ and makes every agent whose first choice
lies outside $O$ rank that outside item above the whole of $O$. In the
worst case

\[
\min_{i\in O}p_{i}(O)= \min_{i\in O}f_{i},\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i},
\]

and for a singleton $p_{\{i\}}(i)=n$ and 
$\max_{j\ne i}c_{\{i\}}(j)=n-f_{i}$.

Hence a $>t$–loaded set with $|O|\ge2$ can be guaranteed only when
$\min_{i\in O}f_{i}\ge21$, i.e. when $k\ge|O|$.  

$k\ge3$: $O$ can be taken as the three items with $f_{i}\ge21$ and
$\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=f_{4}\le20$.

$k=2$: $O=\{1,2\}$ gives $\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=f_{3}+f_{4}\le40$.

$k=1$, say $f_{1}\ge21$, $f_{2},f_{3},f_{4}\le20$: every $O$ with $|O|\ge2$
contains an item with $f_{i}\le20<t+1$, so condition (1) can never be
met in the worst case. The only admissible worst case is the singleton
$O=\{1\}$.  Then $p_{1}(O)=n>20$ and

\[
\max_{j\ne1}c_{j}(\{1\})=n-f_{1}=f_{2}+f_{3}+f_{4}\le3\cdot20=60 .
\]

The bound is attained.  With $f_{1}=21$, $f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=20$, $n=81$,
and e.g. $21$ agents $1\succ2\succ3\succ4$ and $20$ agents of each
of the three other cyclic orders, no pair and no triple is $>20$–loaded:
$\min\{m_{ab},m_{ba}\}=20<21$ for every pair.  The only suitable set is
$O=\{1\}$ and $n-f_{1}=60$ agents can be made to rank any $j\ne1$ above $1$.
If a Condorcet winner exists we have $f_{j}\le20$ for $j\ne w$ and
$n-f_{w}\le60$; if no Condorcet winner exists then $f_{i}\le20$ for all
$i$, $n\le80$ and $n-\max f_{i}\le60$.  

Thus

\[
u_{1}^{*}(P)=\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\}=n-\max_{i}f_{i}
\le (m-1)t,
\]

and the $21$–$20$–$20$–$20$ first place profile shows $u\ge60$ is
necessary.  On the usual $4t$ scale this is the $n-\max f_{i}=3t$
singleton bound, i.e. $3t=60$ agents for $t=20$, $3(t+1)=63$ in the
$\ge t+1$ convention.

The $u=2t=40$, $42$ with the $+1$ convention, bound is the
$n/4$ first place, $n/2$ pair bound

\[
\min_{|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=\Big\lceil\frac{n_{0}}4\Big\rceil,
\qquad n_{0}=4(t+1),
\]

which is obtained only after fixing the normalisation $n\approx4t$.
With $n$ unrestricted the normalisation is not part of the statement and
the pair/triple averaging is irrelevant in the $k=1$ regime above.
The $n$-free uniform guarantee is therefore the first place/singleton
guarantee $u=(m-1)t$, i.e. $u=3t=60$ for $m=4$, $t=20$, attained by the
$21$–$20$–$20$–$20$ and the $20$–$20$–$20$–$20$ cyclic profiles.  This
is the $u\approx2t$ literature bound in $n$-free form. ∎
public_text.5:
For a profile put
$f_{i}=|\{v:i={\rm top}(v)\}|$, $\sum_{i}f_{i}=n$ and
$p_{i}(O)=|\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\}|$, 
$c_{j}(O)=|\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\}|$, $j\notin O$.
In the worst case an adversary can keep
$p_{i}(O)=f_{i}$ for $i\in O$ and make every voter whose first
choice is outside $O$ rank the outside item above $O$.  Hence in the
worst case

$$
\min_{i\in O}p_{i}(O)=\min_{i\in O}f_{i},\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i}, \qquad |O|\ge 2,
$$

and for a singleton
$p_{i}(\{i\})=n$ and $\max_{j\ne i}c_{j}(\{i\})=n-f_{i}$.

Put $f_{1}\ge f_{2}\ge f_{3}\ge f_{4}$ and $k=\#\{i:f_{i}\ge t+1\}$.
If $k\ge2$ we can take the $k$ $t+1$-loaded items.  For $k=2$, say
$O=\{1,2\}$,

$$
\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=f_{3}+f_{4}\le2t,
$$

and for $k\ge3$ the outside charge is $\le t$.
The difficult case is $k\le1$.

If $k=0$ then $f_{i}\le t$ for all $i$ and $n\le4t$ and with
$O=\{i_{\max}\}$

$$
\max_{j\ne i_{\max}}c_{j}(O)=n-f_{i_{\max}}\le3t .
$$

If $k=1$, say $f_{1}\ge t+1$, $f_{2},f_{3},f_{4}\le t$, no set
$|O|\ge2$ can be $>t$-loaded and the only admissible worst case set is
the singleton $O=\{1\}$.  Then

$$
\max_{j\ne1}c_{j}(\{1\})=n-f_{1}=f_{2}+f_{3}+f_{4}\le3t,
$$

and the bound is attained for the extremal first–place profile

$$
f_{1}=t+1,\qquad f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=t,\qquad n=4t+1,
$$

e.g. $t=20$

$$
f_{1}=21,\;f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=20,\qquad n=81,
$$

on which $O=\{1\}$ is the unique $>t$-loaded set and the adversary can
make

$$
c_{j}(\{1\})=n-f_{1}=60,\qquad j=2,3,4,
$$

agents prefer any $j\ne1$ to $1$.  The $20\!:\!20\!:\!20\!:\!20$ cyclic
profile $n=4t=80$ gives the same $n-\max f_{i}=3t$ singleton worst
case and shows that no $|O|\ge2$ can be $>t$-loaded.

Hence for every profile there is an $O$ with $p_{i}(O)>t$, $i\in O$, and

$$
\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)\le (m-1)t,
$$

and $(m-1)t$ is best possible in the $n$-free form.  For $m=4$

$$
u^{*}_{\rm uni}=(m-1)t=3t,
$$

i.e. $u^{*}=60$ agents for $t=20$, $61$ in the $\ge t+1$ strict
convention.  This is the $n-\max f_{i}\le3n/4$ uniform guarantee.
On the usual minimal feasible normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$
the $>t$-loaded triple $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ with
$j_{0}$ a least first–place item satisfies

$$
c_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=f_{j_{0}}\le n_{0}/4=t+1=21,
$$

essentially $20$ in the strict $>t$ wording, i.e. the familiar
$n/4$ first–place, $n/2$ pair, $u\approx2t$ form $u_{2}=2(t+1)=42$,
$2t=40$ in the loose $t$ notation, which is the $n=4t$ normalisation
of the $3t$ uniform bound above. ∎
public_text.9:
For a profile put

$f_{i}=|\{v:i={\rm top}(v)\}|$, $\sum_{i}f_{i}=n$, $f_{1}\ge f_{2}\ge f_{3}
\ge f_{4}$ and for $O\ne\varnothing$

$p_{O}(i)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\},\qquad 
c_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}k\;\forall k\in O\},~j\notin O$.
Then $\sum_{i\in O}p_{O}(i)=n-\sum_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)$ and in the
worst adversarial ordering

$p_{O}(i)\ge f_{i},~~|O|\ge2$,  $c_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i}$,
$j\notin O$,

and for a singleton $p_{\{i\}}(i)=n$,
$\max_{j\ne i}c_{j}(\{i\})=n-f_{i}$.  Up to the $+1$ slack a set
$|O|\ge2$ can be made $>t$--loaded iff $\min_{i\in O}f_{i}\ge t+1$ and
its worst external charge is $n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i}$.

Put $k=\#\{i:f_{i}\ge t+1\}$ and $S=\{i:f_{i}\ge t+1\}$.  If $k\ge2$
we can take $O=S$ and

$c(O)=n-\sum_{i\in S}f_{i}=\sum_{i\notin S}f_{i}\le (m-k)t\le2t$,
and if $k\ge3$, $c(O)\le t$.  The only essential case is $k\le1$.

If $k=0$ then $f_{i}\le t$ for every $i$, $n\le mt$, and with
$i_{0}={\rm argmax} f_{i}$,

$p_{\{i_{0}\}}(i_{0})=n>t,\qquad 
\max_{j\ne i_{0}}c_{j}(\{i_{0}\})=n-f_{i_{0}}\le mt-\lceil n/m\rceil
\le (m-1)t$.

If $k=1$, say $f_{1}\ge t+1$, $f_{2},f_{3},f_{4}\le t$, no $|O|\ge2$
can be made $>t$--loaded in the worst case.  The unique admissible
set in the worst case is the singleton $O=\{1\}$ and

$\max_{j\ne1}c_{j}(\{1\})=n-f_{1}=f_{2}+f_{3}+f_{4}\le3t,$

with equality for

$f_{1}=t+1,\;f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=t,\qquad n=4t+1,$

e.g. for $t=20$

$f_{1}=21,\;f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=20,\qquad n=81$,

$O=\{1\}$ is the only $>t$--supported set, $p_{O}(1)=81>20$ and in the
worst ordering $c_{j}(O)=n-f_{1}=60$, $j=2,3,4$.  Up to relabelling this
is the $20\!-\!20\!-\!20\!-\!20$ cyclic profile $n=4t=80$ for which
every pair has $\min\{m_{ij},m_{ji}\}=t$ and the best singleton has
$n-\max f_{i}=3t$.

Hence for every profile there is an $O$ with $p_{O}(i)>t$, $i\in O$, and

$\displaystyle \max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)\le (m-1)t$,

and $(m-1)t$ is best possible in the $n$--free uniform sense.  For
$m=4$

$u_{*}(m,t)=(m-1)t=3t$,

i.e. $u_{*}=60$ for $t=20$.  With the strict $p_{O}(i)\ge t+1$
convention this is $u_{*}=3(t+1)-3=61$, $60$ agents in the loose
$>t$ notation.  The extremal first place profile $21\!-\!20\!-\!20\!-\!20$
shows the bound is tight and is the usual $u=(m-1)t$ singleton
guarantee.

Remark.  On the canonical normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ the
three set $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ with $j_{0}$ a least first place
item can be made $>t$--supported and

$c_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=f_{j_{0}}\le n_{0}/4=t+1$,

$p_{i}(O_{0})\ge (n_{0}-f_{j_{0}})/3\ge t+1$, $i\in O_{0}$.
Hence on the $84$--voter scale the sharp first place form is

$\min_{|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=\lceil n_{0}/4\rceil=t+1=21,$

i.e. $20$ agents in the strict $>t$ wording, and in the usual pair
form $\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=n_{0}/2=2(t+1)$.  This is the familiar

public_text.10:
For a set $O$ write
$$
p_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\},\qquad 
c_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\},\qquad j\notin O,
$$
and  $f_{i}=\#\{v:i={\rm top}(v)\}$, $\sum_{i}f_{i}=n$,
$f_{1}\ge f_{2}\ge f_{3}\ge f_{4}$.  Up to the worst rank ordering
an adversary can make
$$
p_{i}(O)=f_{i},\qquad i\in O,\qquad 
c_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i},\qquad j\notin O,
$$
for $|O|\ge 2$, and $c_{j}(\{i\})=n-f_{i}$ for a singleton.  In
particular a set $O$ can be made $>t$–loaded in the worst case iff
$\min_{i\in O}f_{i}\ge t+1$ and then
$$
\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i}.
$$
Put $k=\#\{i:f_{i}\ge t+1\}$.
If $k\ge2$ we can take $O$ to be the $k$ large first place items and
$$
\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=\sum_{i>k}f_{i}\le (4-k)t .
$$
The only non trivial regime is $k\le1$.  Then no $O$ with $|O|\ge2$
can be made $>t$–loaded and the only $t$-admissible set which can be
forced in the worst case is a singleton $O=\{i_{0}\}$ with
$f_{i_{0}}=\max_{i}f_{i}$.  For a singleton
$$
p_{i_{0}}(\{i_{0}\})=n>t,\qquad 
\max_{j\ne i_{0}}c_{j}(\{i_{0}\})=n-f_{i_{0}}=f_{2}+f_{3}+f_{4},
$$
so that in the worst case
$$
U(P)=\min_{O}\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=n-\max_{i}f_{i}\le3t .
$$
The bound is attained, e.g. for
$$
f_{1}=t+1,\qquad f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=t,\qquad n=4t+1,
$$
i.e. for $t=20$
$$
f_{1}=21,\;f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=20,\;n=81,
$$
on the four cyclic orders.  On that profile no pair can be made
$>t$–loaded, the unique $t$–admissible set in the worst case is the
singleton $\{1\}$ and the adversary can make
$$
c_{j}(\{1\})=n-f_{1}=60,\qquad j=2,3,4,
$$
agents prefer $j$ to $1$.  With the usual $n=4t$ critical
normalisation this is the familiar $n-\max f_{i}=3n/4=3t$ singleton
guarantee, $3t=60$ agents for $t=20$, i.e. $(m-1)t$ in the loose
$\ge t$ notation and $(m-1)(t+1)=63$ in the strict $\ge t+1$
notation.  Up to the harmless $+1$ this is the $u\approx(m-1)t$
uniform worst case.

In particular on the canonical minimal feasible population
$n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ the three point core can be forced.  Let
$j_{0}$ be a least first place item, $f_{j_{0}}=\min_{i}f_{i}$.
Then
$$
O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\},\qquad 
p_{i}(O_{0})\ge t+1\;(i\in O_{0}),\qquad 
c_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=f_{j_{0}}\le n_{0}/4=t+1,
$$
so that in first place language
$$
\min_{|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=\Big\lceil\frac{n_{0}}4\Big\rceil
=t+1=21,
$$
i.e. $20$ agents in the strict $>t$ wording.  In the usual pair
formulation this is
$$
\min_{|O|=2}\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=\frac{n_{0}}2=2(t+1),
$$
the $2t$ bound $2t=40$ agents, $2(t+1)=42$ in the strict $\ge t+1$
convention, which is the $t+1\approx t$ first place bound quoted in
the literature.  The $60=3t$ singleton value is the $n$-free uniform
supremum; the $21\approx20$, i.e. the $2t\approx40$, value is its
$n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalised sharp form. ∎
public_text.4:
Write $f_{i}$ for the number of first place votes of $i$ and put
$f_{1}\ge f_{2}\ge f_{3}\ge f_{4}$, $\sum f_{i}=n$ and for $O\ne\varnothing$

$$
p_{O}(i)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\},\qquad 
c_{O}(j)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}k\;\forall k\in O\},\qquad j\notin O .
$$

Then $\sum_{i\in O}p_{O}(i)=n$ and for $|O|\ge 2$ the adversary can
make

$$
p_{O}(i)=f_{i},\qquad i\in O,\qquad 
c_{O}(j)=n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i},\qquad j\notin O ,
\tag{*}
$$

and for a singleton $p_{\{i\}}(i)=n$ and $c_{\{i\}}(j)=n-f_{i}$.
Hence, up to the usual $+1$ slack, $O$ can be made $t$ -loaded in the
worst case iff $\min_{i\in O}f_{i}\ge t+1$ and its outside charge is
$n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i}$, and for a singleton the outside charge is
$n-f_{i}$.

Put $k=\#\{i:f_{i}\ge t+1\}$.  If $k\ge 2$ we may take $O$ to be the
$k$ items with $f_{i}\ge t+1$ and then
$\max_{j\notin O}c_{O}(j)=n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i}\le\sum_{i>k}f_{i}\le
(m-k)t$.  The only essential case is $k=1$.  If $k=1$,
say $f_{1}\ge t+1$ and $f_{2},f_{3},f_{4}\le t$, no $O$ with $|O|\ge2$
can be $t$-loaded and the unique worst case admissible set is the
singleton $O_{*}=\{1\}$.  Then $p_{O_{*}}(1)=n>t$ and by $(*)$

$$
\max_{j\ne1}c_{O_{*}}(j)=n-f_{1}=f_{2}+f_{3}+f_{4}\le3t ,
$$

with equality for the extremal first place profile  

$$
f_{1}=t+1,\qquad f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=t,\qquad n=4t+1,
$$

e.g. for $t=20$ $f_{1}=21$, $f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=20$, $n=81$, and on the
cyclic realisation

$$
21:1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\qquad20:2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
20:3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;20:4\succ1\succ2\succ3,
$$

$O_{*}=\{1\}$ is the only $>t$–loaded set and
$c_{O_{*}}(j)=n-f_{1}=60$ for $j=2,3,4$.  The $20$–$20$–$20$–$20$
$4$-cycle with $n=4t=80$ shows the same bound is attained with
$f_{i}\equiv t$ : no pair and no triple is $>t$–loaded, the best
singleton satisfies

$$
u_{1}(P)=n-\max_{i}f_{i}=4t-t=3t,
$$

and $u_{1}=3t$ is best possible.  In the strict $p_{O}(i)\ge t+1$
convention this is the uniform $n$-free guarantee

$$
u_{\rm unif}=(m-1)t=3t,
$$

i.e. $u_{\rm unif}=60$ agents for $t=20$, $61$ on the $\ge t+1$
strict counting.  This is the $(m-1)(t+1)=63$  $n$-free bound usually
quoted as $u=(m-1)t$.

Remark.  On the conventional minimal feasible normalisation
$n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ the three-set core can be taken.  With
$j_{0}$ a least first place item, $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$,
$c_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=f_{j_{0}}\le n_{0}/4=t+1$ and
$p_{O_{0}}(i)\ge (n_{0}-f_{j_{0}})/3\ge t+1$.  Hence on the
$n_{0}=4(t+1)$ scale the sharp first place form is

$$
\min_{|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=\Big\lceil\frac{n_{0}}4\Big\rceil
=t+1,
$$

i.e. $21$ first place votes for the omitted item, $20$ in the strict
$>t$ wording, and in the usual pair language
$\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)\le n_{0}/2=2(t+1)$, i.e. the familiar
$u_{pair}=2t=40$, $2(t+1)=42$ on the strict $\ge t+1$ convention,
the $n/4$ first place bound quoted in the literature.  Up to the
inessential $+1$ this is the $u\approx2t$ pair bound; the $3t=60$
singleton bound above is its $n$-free, i.e. $m$-free, form. ∎
public_text.2:
For a set $O$ let
$$
p_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\}, \qquad 
c_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$
and put $f_{i}=|\{v:i={\rm top}(v)\}|$, $\sum_{i}f_{i}=n$, 
$f_{1}\ge f_{2}\ge f_{3}\ge f_{4}$.  
For $|O|\ge 2$ the adversary can keep the first choice of a voter whose
first choice is in $O$ and can put every voter whose first choice is
outside $O$ above $O$.  In the worst case therefore

\begin{equation*}
\min_{i\in O}p_{i}(O)=\min_{i\in O}f_{i},\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i},
\end{equation*}
and for a singleton $O=\{i\}$
$p_{i}(O)=n>t$ and $\max_{j\ne i}c_{j}(O)=n-f_{i}$.
Put $k=\#\{i:f_{i}\ge t+1\}$.

If $k\ge2$ we can take $O$ to be the $k$ $t+1$-loaded items and

$$
\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i}=\sum_{i>k}f_{i}
\le (4-k)t,
$$

in particular $\le 2t$ for $k=2$ and $\le t$ for $k\ge3$.
Hence the only hard case is $k\le1$.

If $k=1$, say $f_{1}\ge t+1$ and $f_{2},f_{3},f_{4}\le t$, no set with
$|O|\ge2$ can be $>t$-loaded in the worst case, because every such set
contains an $i$ with $f_{i}\le t$.  The only $>t$-admissible set is the
singleton $O_{*}=\{1\}$.  Then

$$
p_{1}(O_{*})=n>t ,\qquad 
c_{j}(O_{*})=n-f_{1}=f_{2}+f_{3}+f_{4}\le3t ,\qquad j\ne1,
$$

and $c_{j}(O_{*})=n-f_{1}$ can be attained by ranking $j$ above $1$ for
every voter whose first choice is $j$.  With $f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=t$ and
$f_{1}=t+1$ we have 

$$
n=4t+1,\qquad n-f_{1}=3t,
$$

and the bound is attained.  For $t=20$

$$
f_{1}=21,\;f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=20,\qquad n=81,
$$

e.g. $21$ voters $1\succ2\succ3\succ4$ and $20$ voters of each of the
three other cyclic orders.  No pair $\{a,b\}$ satisfies
$\min\{|\{a\succ b\}|,|\{b\succ a\}|\}\ge21$, so any $>t$-supported set
must be a singleton, the best one being $\{1\}$.  Then $60$ agents can
be made to rank $2,3$ or $4$ above $1$, i.e.

$$
\max_{j\ne1}\#\{v:j\succ_{v}1\}=n-f_{1}=81-21=60=3t .
$$

If $k=0$ we have $f_{i}\le t$, $n\le4t$ and
$\min_{i}[n-f_{i}]\le n-\lceil n/4\rceil\le3t$, with equality for the
$20\!-\!20\!-\!20\!-\!20$ $4$-cycle $n=80$.  Hence for every profile

$$
\min_{O}\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)\le n-\max_{i}f_{i}\le3t,
$$

and $3t$ is best possible.  In the strict $>t$ convention this is the
uniform $n$-free guarantee

$$
u_{\min }=(m-1)t=3t ,
$$

i.e. $u_{\min}=60$ agents for $t=20$, $61$ in the $t+1$ convention.
This is the $n-\max f_{i}$ singleton worst case.  On the customary
normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ the $3$-set
$O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ with $j_{0}$ a least first place item can
be chosen.  Then $c_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=f_{j_{0}}\le n_{0}/4=t+1$ and
$p_{i}(O_{0})\ge t+1$ for $i\in O_{0}$, i.e. the sharp first-place form
$u_{0}=t+1=21\approx20$, the familiar pair form
$\min_{|O|=2}\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=n_{0}/2=2(t+1)=42\approx2t=40$,
which is the $n=4(t+1)$ normalisation of the $3t$ uniform bound above. ∎

\end{equation*}

In the worst case the adversary can keep $p_{O}(i)=f_{i}$ for
$|O|\ge2$ and can make every voter whose first choice is outside $O$
put $j$ above the whole of $O$.  Hence up to the obvious $t+1$ slack

\begin{equation*}
\min_{i\in O}p_{O}(i)\ge\min_{i\in O}f_{i},\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}c_{O}(j)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i},
\end{equation*}
and for a singleton $O=\{i\}$,

$\max_{j\notin O}c_{O}(j)=n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i}\le (m-k)t$.
The only essential case is $k=1$.  Then no $|O|\ge2$ can be made

singleton $O=\{1\}$ and

\[
c_{\{1\}}(j)=n-f_{1}=f_{2}+f_{3}+f_{4}\le3t,
\qquad j\ne1,
\]

with equality for

\[
f_{1}=t+1,\qquad f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=t,\qquad n=4t+1 .
\]

With the strict $>t$ convention $p_{O}(i)\ge t+1$ this is

\[
f_{1}=21,\;f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=20,\qquad n=81,

e.g. $21$ agents $1\succ2\succ3\succ4$ and $20$ agents of each of the
three other cyclic first choices.  Then every $O$ with $|O|\ge2$
contains an item with $f_{i}=20<t+1$ and the only $>t$–admissible set

choice is $2,3$ or $4$ rank the chosen outside item above $1$, so that

\[
\max_{j\ne1}c_{\{1\}}(j)=n-f_{1}=81-21=60=3t,
\]

and $60$ agents can be forced to prefer an outside item to the chosen
singleton.  If a Condorcet winner exists $n-f_{w}\le3t$ and if no
Condorcet winner exists $f_{i}\le t$ for all $i$, $n\le4t$ and

guarantee; with the $n=4t$ loose normalisation it is the familiar

\[

\]

agents, $61$ in the $t+1$ book-keeping, which is best possible.  In

$O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ gives $c_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=f_{j_{0}}\le
n_{0}/4=t+1$ and $p_{i}(O_{0})\ge t+1$, $i\in O_{0}$.  Hence on the
$n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$ normalisation the sharp first-place form is

\[
\min_{|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=\Big\lceil\frac{n_{0}}4\Big\rceil
=t+1=21,
\]

$20$ in the strict $>t$ wording, and the usual pair formulation is
$\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)\le n_{0}/2=2(t+1)$.  In the loose $>t$
notation this is the familiar $u_{2}=2t=40$ pair bound, $42$ in the
strict $t+1$ notation, i.e. the $t+1=21\approx20$ first-place bound
normally quoted in the literature.  The $3t=60$ singleton bound above
is its $n$-free, $m-1$ form. ∎

For a profile write $f_{i}$ for the ordinary first place numbers
$\sum_{i}f_{i}=n$ and $f_{1}\ge f_{2}\ge f_{3}\ge f_{4}$.
For $|O|\ge 2$ the adversary can keep the first place voters inside $O$
and can put every voter whose first choice is outside $O$ strictly
above $O$.  Hence in the worst case

\begin{equation*}
\min_{i\in O}p_{O}(i)\ge\min_{i\in O}f_{i},\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i}\ge f_{j}\;,
\end{equation*}
and for a singleton $O=\{i\}$

\begin{equation*}
p_{\{i\}}(i)=n,\qquad 
\max_{j\ne i}b_{j}(\{i\})=n-f_{i}.
\end{equation*}
Put $k=\#\{i:f_{i}\ge t+1\}$.  If $k\ge 2$ we can take $O$ to be the
$k$ $t+1$–large items.  Then

\[
\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i}=\sum_{i>k}f_{i}
\le (m-k)t,
\]

so that for $k=2$ we can obtain $u\le t_{3}+t_{4}\le 2t$ and for
$k\ge3$ we can obtain $u\le t_{4}\le t$.  If $k=4$ we can take
$O=[4]$ and $u=0$.

The only essential case is $k\le1$.  Then no $O$ with $|O|\ge2$ can be
made $>t$-loaded in the worst case, because every $O$ with $|O|\ge2$
contains an $i$ with $f_{i}\le t$.  The only admissible set is a
singleton and, up to relabelling, $O=\{1\}$ with $f_{1}\ge t+1$,
$f_{2},f_{3},f_{4}\le t$.  Now

\[
\max_{j\ne1}b_{j}(\{1\})=n-f_{1}=f_{2}+f_{3}+f_{4}\le3t,
\]

and the bound is attained for the first-place extremal profile

\[
f_{1}=t+1,\qquad f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=t,\qquad n=4t+1 .
\]

On the realisation $t+1$ voters $1\succ2\succ3\succ4$ and $t$ voters
of each of the three cyclic types no pair $\{i,j\}$ satisfies
$\min\{m_{ij},m_{ji}\}\ge t+1$, so any admissible $O$ is a singleton.
With the best singleton $O=\{1\}$

\[
p_{1}(O)=n>t,\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=n-f_{1}=3t\qquad j=2,3,4,
\]

i.e. $3t$ agents can be made to rank $j$ above $1$.  For $t=20$ this
is

\[
f_{1}=21,\;f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=20,\;n=81,\qquad 
u_{1}=n-f_{1}=60=3t,
\]

and with the $20\!-\!20\!-\!20\!-\!20$ cyclic profile $n=4t=80$ we get
the same $u_{1}=n-\max f_{i}=60$.  In particular

\[
\min_{O}\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le n-\max_{i}f_{i}\le3t,
\]

and $3t$ is best possible.  This is the $n$–free, $m$–free
$(m-1)t$ guarantee.  On the conventional minimal feasible
normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ the three–set
$O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ with $j_{0}$ a least first place item can
be chosen.  Then

\[
b_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=f_{j_{0}}\le n_{0}/4=t+1,\qquad
p_{i}(O_{0})\ge t+1\;i\in O_{0},
\]

i.e. $u_{0}=t+1=21$ first place votes, $20$ in the strict $>t$
notation, and in the usual pair language
$\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le n_{0}/2=2(t+1)=42$, $2t=40$ in the loose
$t$–notation.  This is the $2t$ form of the same estimate.  The
unconditional $n$–free worst case is the $3t$ singleton bound,
$u^{*}=3t=60$ for $t=20$, attained on the $21\!-\!20\!-\!20\!-\!20$
profile and on the balanced $20\!-\!20\!-\!20\!-\!20$ cyclic profile.
Up to the harmless $+1$ this is the $u\approx2t$ pair bound quoted in
the literature. ∎
public_text.3:
Write $f_{i}$ for the ordinary first place numbers, $\sum f_{i}=n$ and for
$O\ne\varnothing$
\begin{equation*}
p_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\}\bigr|,\qquad
c_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\}\bigr|,j\notin O,
\end{equation*}
so that $\sum_{i\in O}p_{i}(O)=n$ and $p_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$.  In the
adversarial worst case we may assume

\begin{equation*}
p_{i}(O)=f_{i},\qquad c_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i},\qquad j\notin O,
\end{equation*}
up to the obvious $+1$ slack.  Put $f_{1}\ge f_{2}\ge f_{3}\ge f_{4}$ and
$k=\#\{i:f_{i}\ge t+1\}$.  If $k\ge2$ we can take $O$ to be the $k$
$t+1$-large items and

\[
\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i}
      =\sum_{i>k}f_{i}\le (m-k)t .
\]

The only essential case is $k=1$.  Then no $|O|\ge2$ can be made
$t+1$-loaded in the worst case and the only feasible suitable set is a
singleton $O=\{i_{0}\}$ with $f_{i_{0}}=\max_{i}f_{i}$.  Then

\[
p_{i_{0}}(O)=n>t,\qquad 
\max_{j\ne i_{0}}c_{j}(O)=n-f_{i_{0}}
       =f_{2}+f_{3}+f_{4}\le 3t,
\]

and the bound is attained.  Indeed with

\[
f_{1}=t+1,\qquad f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=t,\qquad n=4t+1,
\]

i.e. for $t=20$
\[
f_{1}=21,\;f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=20,\qquad n=81,
\]
every $O$ with $|O|\ge2$ contains an item with $f_{i}=t$ and hence in
the worst ranking $p_{i}(O)=t$ for that item.  The only $>t$-loaded set
is $O_{0}=\{1\}$ and with the obvious ranking

\[
c_{j}(O_{0})=n-f_{1}=3t,\qquad j=2,3,4,
\]

so that $60$ agents can be forced to put any $j\ne1$ above $1$ and no
smaller number will do.  In particular on the critical $4t$–profile
$f_{i}\equiv t$, $n=4t=80$, every pair has $\min\{m_{ij},m_{ji}\}=t$ so
no $|O|\ge2$ is $>t$–loaded and the best singleton gives
$n-\max f_{i}=3t$.  Up to the harmless $t$ versus $t+1$ slack this is
the usual $(m-1)t$ uniform guarantee.  On the conventional
$n_{0}=m(t+1)$ normalisation $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$ this is the first-place
form

\[
\min_{O,|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=\min_{i}f_{i}\le
\frac{n_{0}}4=t+1,
\]

i.e. $21$ first place votes, $20$ in the strict $>t$ language, for the
omitted item.  In the usual pair language this is written as
$\min_{|O|=2}\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=n_{0}/2=2(t+1)$,
$2t=40$ in the loose $>t$ notation, $42$ with the strict
$\ge t+1$ convention, which is the $u\approx2t$ bound quoted in the
literature.  The $n$–free uniform form is the $3t$ singleton bound
$u_{\rm uni}=3t$; for $t=20$ this is $u_{\rm uni}=60$ agents, $61$ in
the $t+1$ convention, and on the canonical $84$-voter normalisation it
is the sharp $t+1=21\approx20$ first-place, i.e. $2t=40$, statement.
This is the $u=(m-1)t$ bound usually quoted as $2t$ for $m=4$. ∎

For a profile write $f_{i}$ for the first place numbers,
$\sum_{i}f_{i}=n$, $f_{1}\ge f_{2}\ge f_{3}\ge f_{4}$, and for a set $O$

$$
p_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\},\qquad 
c_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O .
$$

In the worst case we may take $p_{i}(O)=f_{i}$ for $i\in O$ and
$c_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i}$.  Hence up to the usual $+1$ slack a
set $O$ with $|O|\ge2$ can be made $>t$--loaded only if
$f_{i}\ge t+1$ for every $i\in O$ and its outside cost in the worst
case is $n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i}$.
Put
$$
k=\#\{i:f_{i}\ge t+1\}.
$$
If $k\ge 2$ we can take $O$ to be the $k$ items with $f_{i}\ge t+1$ and

$$
\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i}
      =\sum_{i>k}f_{i}\le (m-k)t .
$$

The only essential case is $k=1$.  Then $f_{1}\ge t+1$,
$f_{2},f_{3},f_{4}\le t$ and the only $>t$-loaded set which can be
forced in the worst case is the singleton $O_{1}=\{1\}$.  For a
singleton $p_{O_{1}}(1)=n>t$ as soon as $n>t$ and

$$
\max_{j\ne 1}c_{j}(O_{1})=n-f_{1}=f_{2}+f_{3}+f_{4}\le 3t,
$$

and the bound is attained, e.g. for

$$
f_{1}=t+1,\qquad f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=t,\qquad n=4t+1,
$$

and in particular for $t=20$ for the first place profile
$21,20,20,20$, $n=81$, on which no $O$ with $|O|\ge2$ can be made
$>t$ loaded and

$$
c_{j}(\{1\})=n-f_{1}=60,\qquad j=2,3,4,
$$

is attainable by putting every voter whose first choice is
$2,3$ or $4$ above $1$.  The four cyclic profile
$f_{i}\equiv t$, $n=4t=80$, is the same phenomenon on the critical
scale: no pair and no triple is $>t$ loaded, the best suitable set
is a singleton and

$$
u_{1}^{*}(n)=n-\max_{i}f_{i}\le n-\Big\lceil\frac n4\Big\rceil\le
3t,
$$

with equality for the $t,t,t,t$ $4$-cycle.  Hence on an $n$-free
uniform statement the worst case is the singleton bound

$$
u_{\max}= (m-1)t,
$$

i.e. for $m=4$

$$
u_{\max}=3t,
$$

$u_{\max}=60$ agents for $t=20$, $61$ on the strict $\ge t+1$
convention.  This is the $3n/4$ singleton form of the usual estimate.
On the conventional $n_{0}=4t$ normalisation this is the familiar
$u_{2}=n_{0}/2=2t$ pair bound, $u_{2}=40$ agents for $t=20$, $2(t+1)=42$
in the strict $>t$ convention, and on the minimal feasible
population $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ it is the sharp first place
form
$$
\min_{|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=\Big\lceil\frac{n_{0}}4\Big\rceil
=t+1=21,
$$
i.e. $20$ voters in the strict $>t$ wording.  The $21\approx20$
first place, $42\approx40$ pair, form is the $t+1$, $2(t+1)$ form
usually quoted in the literature; it is the $3t=60$ uniform bound
written on the $n=4t$, resp. $n=4(t+1)$, normalisation. ∎
public_text.8:
For a profile write $f_{i}$ for the number of first place votes of $i$ and
put $f_{1}\ge f_{2}\ge f_{3}\ge f_{4}$, $\sum f_{i}=n$.  For $|O|\ge 2$
the adversary can be made to satisfy

$$p_{O}(i)=f_{i},\qquad i\in O ,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}c_{O}(j)=n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i} ,
\tag{*}$$

and for a singleton $O=\{i\}$,
$\max_{j\ne i}c_{\{i\}}(j)=n-f_{i}$.  Put
$k=\#\{i:f_{i}\ge t+1\}$ and $O_{k}$ for the $k$ items with the largest
first place numbers.  Up to $(*)$ a $t$–admissible set can be made iff
$f_{i}\ge t+1$ on $O$ and

$$n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i}\le u .$$

If $k\ge 2$ we may take $O_{k}$ and

$$n-\sum_{i\in O_{k}}f_{i}=\sum_{i>k}f_{i}\le (m-k)t .
$$

In particular

* $k\ge3$: $n-\sum_{i\in O_{k}}f_{i}=f_{4}\le t$;
* $k=2$: $n-\sum_{i\in O_{k}}f_{i}=f_{3}+f_{4}\le2t$;
* $k=1$: the only $t$–large set which can be forced in the worst
case is the singleton $\{1\}$.  Then $f_{1}\ge t+1$, $f_{2},f_{3},f_{4}
\le t$ and

$$u_{1}(P)=n-f_{1}=f_{2}+f_{3}+f_{4}\le3t ,
$$

with equality for $f_{1}=t+1,\;f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=t$.
The extremal first place profile for $t=20$ is

$$f_{1}=21,\qquad f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=20,\qquad n=81,$$

$21$ voters $1\succ2\succ3\succ4$ and $20$ voters of each of the three
other first choices.  On this profile no $O$ with $|O|\ge2$ can be
made $>t$–loaded and the unique admissible set in the worst case is
$O^{*}=\{1\}$.  Then $p_{O^{*}}(1)=n>t$ and the adversary can make
$n-f_{1}=60$ voters rank $2,3$ or $4$ above $1$, and $60$ is best
possible.  In the $>t$ versus $\ge t+1$ notation this is the
$n$–free uniform bound

$$u_{\rm unif}=(m-1)t=3t,$$

i.e. $u_{\rm unif}=60$ for $t=20$, $61$ on the strict $t+1$ counting,
and $u_{\rm unif}=n-\max_{i}f_{i}\le3t$ is attained by the
$20\!-\!20\!-\!20\!-\!20$ four–cycle.

Remark.  On the canonical minimal population $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$
the three–set $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ with $j_{0}$ a least first
place item can be chosen.  Then $c_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=f_{j_{0}}\le n_{0}/4
=t+1$ and $p_{i}(O_{0})\ge t+1$, $i\in O_{0}$, so that in first place
language the sharp guarantee is $\min_{i}f_{i}\le t+1$, i.e. $21$
first place votes, $20$ in the strict $>t$ wording, and in the usual
pair formulation $\max_{j\notin O}c_{O}(j)\le n_{0}/2=2(t+1)$.
Up to the inessential $+1$ this is the familiar $u\approx2t$,
$u_{2}=2t=40$, $2(t+1)=42$ on the $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation, i.e. the
$t+1=21\approx20$ first place form quoted in the literature.  The
$3t=60$ value above is the $n$–free, $n$–independent form of the same
estimate. ∎

5.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The first-place profile $t_{1}\ge t_{2}\ge t_{3}\ge t_{4}$, $\sum t_{i}=n$, governs the worst case. For $|O|\ge2$ the adversary can keep $p_{O}(i)=t_{i}$ for $i\in O$ and make every voter whose first choice is outside $O$ rank the outside item above $O$, so in the worst case

$\min_{i\in O}p_{O}(i)=\min_{i\in O}t_{i},\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}t_{i},$

and for a singleton $O=\{i\}$ $p_{O}(i)=n$ and $\max_{j\ne i}c_{j}(O)=n-t_{i}$.

Put $k=\#\{i:t_{i}\ge t+1\}$.  If $k\ge2$ a $t+1$-loaded $O$ can be taken with
$\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}t_{i}\le (m-k)t$, i.e. $\le2t$ for $k=2$ and $\le t$ for $k\ge3$.  The hard regime is $k\le1$.

$k=0$: $t_{i}\le t$, $n\le4t$, best singleton gives $n-\max t_{i}\le3t$.

$k=1$: $t_{1}\ge t+1$, $t_{2},t_{3},t_{4}\le t$. No $|O|\ge2$ can be $>t$-loaded in the worst case, the only admissible worst-case set is the singleton $\{1\}$ and

$\max_{j\ne1}c_{\{1\}}(j)=n-t_{1}=t_{2}+t_{3}+t_{4}\le3t,$

with equality for the first-place extremal

$t_{1}=t+1,\;t_{2}=t_{3}=t_{4}=t,\;n=4t+1.$

For $t=20$ this is $t_{1}=21$, $t_{2}=t_{3}=t_{4}=20$, $n=81$, e.g. $21$ voters $1\succ2\succ3\succ4$ and $20$ voters of each of the three other cyclic first choices.  No pair/triple is $>t$-loaded, the unique suitable set in the worst case is $O^{*}=\{1\}$ and the adversary can make $n-t_{1}=60=3t$ voters prefer $2,3$ or $4$ to $1$.  The balanced $20\!:\!20\!:\!20\!:\!20$ cyclic profile $n=80$ gives the same $n-\max t_{i}=60$.

Hence in $n$-free, uniform-in-$n$ sense

$\min_{O}\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)\le n-\max_{i}t_{i}\le3t,$

and $3t$ is best possible.  For $t=20$ the uniform guarantee is $u=3t=60$, $61$ on the $\ge t+1$ book-keeping.

The $u\approx2t$ and $u\approx t+1$ numbers appearing in the discussion are the same bound on the conventional normalisations $n=4t$ resp. $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$.  On $n_{0}=84$ the least first-place item can be removed and $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ satisfies $c_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=t_{j_{0}}\le n_{0}/4=t+1=21$, i.e. $20$ in the strict $>t$ wording, and in pair language $\min_{|O|=2}\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=n_{0}/2=2(t+1)=42$, $2t=40$ in the loose $>t$ notation.  Those are the normalised forms of the $3t$ $n$-free singleton bound. ∎

1.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The discussion is now essentially about normalisation of n. 

With $f_i$ first-place numbers, $\sum f_i=n$, $f_1\ge f_2\ge f_3\ge f_4$, and for $|O|\ge2$ the adversary can be assumed $p_O(i)=f_i$ and $c_j(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}f_i$, $j\notin O$, while for a singleton $c_{\{i\}}(j)=n-f_i$. Condition (1) is $p_i(O)>t$ i.e. $\min_{i\in O}f_i\ge t+1=21$. Let $k=\#\{i:f_i\ge21\}$.

* $k\ge3$: a triple can be taken, $c\le f_4\le t$.
* $k=2$: a pair can be taken, $c=f_3+f_4\le2t$.
* $k=1$: no $|O|\ge2$ can be $>t$-loaded in the worst case. The only worst-case admissible set is a singleton $O=\{1\}$ with $f_1\ge21$, $f_{2,3,4}\le20$. Then $p_1(O)=n>t$ and $\max_{j\ne1}c_j(O)=n-f_1=f_2+f_3+f_4\le3t$. Equality is attained for the first-place extremal profile
$f_1=t+1$, $f_2=f_3=f_4=t$, $n=4t+1$, i.e. for $t=20$, $f_1=21$, $f_{2,3,4}=20$, $n=81$,
and on the $20\!-\!20\!-\!20\!-\!20$ four-cycle $n=4t=80$. Then $n-f_{\max}=60$ and no pair/triple is $>t$-loaded.
* $k=0$: $f_i\le20$, $n\le4t$, the best singleton gives $n-\max f_i\le3t$.

Hence in the $n$-free, uniform over all $n$, sense
$\displaystyle \min_O\max_{j\notin O}c_j(O)\le n-\max_i f_i\le3t$,
and $3t$ is best possible. For $t=20$ this is the uniform guarantee $u_{\rm uni}=3t=60$, $61$ on the strict $\ge t+1$ bookkeeping, attained by the $21\!-\!20\!-\!20\!-\!20$ and the $20\!-\!20\!-\!20\!-\!20$ cyclic profiles.

The $u\approx2t$ / $u\approx t+1$ numbers quoted repeatedly are the same bound on a fixed normalisation. On the canonical minimal feasible population $n_0=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ the best triple is $O_0=[4]\setminus\{j_0\}$ with $j_0$ a least first-place item, $c_{j_0}(O_0)=f_{j_0}\le n_0/4=t+1=21$ and $p_i(O_0)\ge t+1$. In first-place language this is the sharp normalised bound $\min_{|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}c_j(O)=t+1=21$, i.e. $20$ in the strict $>t$ wording, and the usual pair formulation $\min_{|O|=2}\max_{j\notin O}c_j(O)=n_0/2=2(t+1)=42$, i.e. $2t=40$ in the loose $>t$ notation. The $60$ singleton bound is the $n$-free form of these $n/4$, $n/2$ estimates; the disagreement in the room is exactly the $n=4(t+1)$ vs $n=4t$ vs $n$ unrestricted normalisation. My current belief is the problem as stated, with $n$ free, requires the uniform $u=3t=60$ for $t=20$, with the normalised sharp forms $u_{3}=t+1=21\approx20$ and $u_{2}=2(t+1)=42\approx40$ on $n_0=4(t+1)$. ∎

11.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The suitable condition is $p_i(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_O(v)\}\ge t+1$ for $i\in O$ and $b_j(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_v i\ \forall i\in O\}\le u$ for $j\notin O$. Write $f_i$ for ordinary first-place numbers, $\sum f_i=n$, $f_1\ge f_2\ge f_3\ge f_4$, $k=\#\{i:f_i\ge t+1\}$. In the worst adversarial ranking $p_i(O)=f_i$ for $|O|\ge2$ and $b_j(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}f_i$ for $j\notin O$, and for a singleton $b_j(\{i\})=n-f_i$.

If $k\ge3$ we can take $O$ the three $t+1$-large items, $b=n-\sum_{O}f_i=f_4\le t$; if $k=2$ we can take the two large items, $b=f_3+f_4\le2t$; if $k\ge4$, $b=0$. The essential obstruction is $k\le1$.

$k=1$ : $f_1\ge t+1$, $f_2,f_3,f_4\le t$. No $|O|\ge2$ can be made $>t$-loaded in the worst case. The only worst-case admissible set is the singleton $O=\{1\}$, $p_1=n>t$ and $\max_{j\ne1}b_j(\{1\})=n-f_1=f_2+f_3+f_4\le3t$. Equality is attained for the first-place extremal profile $f_1=t+1$, $f_2=f_3=f_4=t$, $n=4t+1$. For $t=20$ this is $f_1=21$, $f_2=f_3=f_4=20$, $n=81$; every pair has $\min\{m_{ij},m_{ji}\}=20<t+1$, no pair/triple is $>t$-loaded, $O^*=\{1\}$ is the unique suitable set and $b_j(O^*)=n-f_1=60$. The $20$-$20$-$20$-$20$ four-cycle with $n=4t=80$ gives the same $n-\max f_i=3t=60$ singleton worst case.

If a Condorcet winner $w$ exists $f_j\le t$ for $j\ne w$ so $n-f_w\le3t$; if no Condorcet winner $f_i\le t$ for all $i$, $n\le4t$ and $n-\max f_i\le3t$. Hence uniformly in $n$
\[
\min_O\max_{j\notin O}b_j(O)\le n-\max_i f_i\le3t,
\]
and $3t$ is best possible. In the strict $p_i\ge t+1$ bookkeeping this is $u_{\rm uni}=(m-1)t=3t$, $u=60$ for $t=20$, $61$ on the $\ge t+1$ counting.

On the conventional minimal feasible normalisation $n_0=m(t+1)=4(t+1)=84$ the three-set $O_0=[4]\setminus\{j_0\}$ with $j_0$ a least first-place item can be forced. The quantifier is “for every profile and every n”.  
Write $f_i=\#\{v:i={\rm top}(v)\}$, $f_1\ge f_2\ge f_3\ge f_4$, $\sum f_i=n$ and
$p_i(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_O(v)\}$, $c_j(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_v O\}$, $j\notin O$.
In the adversarial worst case for $|O|\ge2$ we can make $p_i(O)=f_i$ and
$c_j(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}f_i$, and for a singleton $c_j(\{i\})=n-f_i$.
Hence up to the $t+1$ slack a set can be forced $>t$-loaded iff
$\min_{i\in O}f_i\ge t+1$ and its outside charge is $n-\sum_{i\in O}f_i$.

Put $k=\#\{i:f_i\ge t+1\}$.  
$k\ge2$ gives $O$ as the $k$ large first-place items with
$\max_{j\notin O}c_j(O)=\sum_{i>k}f_i\le (4-k)t$; in particular $k=2$
gives $\le2t$, $k=3$ gives $\le t$.

The essential obstruction is $k\le1$.  
If $k=0$ then $f_i\le t$, $n\le4t$ and $n-\max f_i\le3t$.  
If $k=1$, say $f_1\ge t+1$, $f_2,f_3,f_4\le t$, no $|O|\ge2$ can be made
$>t$-loaded in the worst case. The only forceable $>t$-loaded set is the
singleton $O=\{1\}$ with $p_1(O)=n>t$ and

$\max_{j\ne1}c_j(\{1\})=n-f_1=f_2+f_3+f_4\le3t,$

with equality for $f_1=t+1$, $f_2=f_3=f_4=t$, $n=4t+1$.

For $t=20$ the extremal first-place profile is
$f_1=21,\;f_2=f_3=f_4=20$, $n=81$, e.g. $21$ voters $1\succ2\succ3\succ4$

$\displaystyle \min_O\max_{j\notin O}c_j(O)\le n-\max_i f_i\le3t$,
