For a profile let

$f_{i}=|\{v:i={\rm top}(v)\}|$, $f_{1}\ge f_{2}\ge f_{3}\ge f_{4}$,
$\sum f_{i}=n$, and for $O\ne\varnothing$

$$
p_{O}(i)=\bigl|\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\}\bigr|,\qquad 
c_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{v:j\succ_{v}k\;\forall k\in O\}\bigr| ,\qquad j\notin O .
$$

For $|O|\ge 2$ the adversary can keep $p_{O}(i)=f_{i},\,i\in O$, and can
make every voter whose first choice is outside $O$ rank the outside
item above $O$.  In the worst case

$$
\min_{i\in O}p_{O}(i)=\min_{i\in O}f_{i},\qquad
\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=n-\sum_{i\in O}f_{i},
$$

and for a singleton

$$
p_{\{i\}}(i)=n,\qquad 
\max_{j\ne i}c_{j}(\{i\})=n-f_{i}.
$$

Put $k=\#\{i:f_{i}\ge t+1\}$.  If $k\ge2$ we can take $O$ to be the $k$
$t+1$–large items and

$$
\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=\sum_{i>k}f_{i}\le (4-k)t,
$$

so that $k=2$ gives $\le f_{3}+f_{4}\le 2t$ and $k\ge3$ gives $\le t$.
The only $n$-free obstruction is $k\le1$.

If $k=0$, $f_{i}\le t$, $n\le4t$ and with $i_{0}=\arg\max f_{i}$

$$
\max_{j\ne i_{0}}c_{j}(\{i_{0}\})=n-f_{i_{0}}\le3t .
$$

If $k=1$, say $f_{1}\ge t+1$, $f_{2},f_{3},f_{4}\le t$, no $|O|\ge2$ can
be made $>t$-loaded in the worst case and the only worst-case
admissible set is the singleton $O_{*}=\{1\}$.  Then

$$
p_{O_{*}}(1)=n>t,\qquad 
\max_{j\ne1}c_{j}(O_{*})=n-f_{1}=f_{2}+f_{3}+f_{4}\le3t,
$$

and the bound is attained for

$$
f_{1}=t+1,\qquad f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=t,\qquad n=4t+1 .
$$

For $t=20$

$$
f_{1}=21,\;f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=20,\qquad n=81,
$$

e.g. $21$ voters $1\succ2\succ3\succ4$ and $20$ voters of each of the
three other cyclic orders.  No pair has $\min\{m_{ab},m_{ba}\}\ge t+1$,
so no $|O|\ge2$ can be made $>t$-loaded; the unique $>t$-admissible set
in the worst case is $O^{*}=\{1\}$ and in the worst ordering

$$
c_{j}(O^{*})=n-f_{1}=81-21=60=3t,\qquad j=2,3,4,
$$

so $60$ agents can be forced to rank $2,3$ or $4$ above $1$, and
$p_{O^{*}}(1)=81>t$.  The $20\!-\!20\!-\!20\!-\!20$ four-cycle $n=4t=80$
gives the same $n-\max f_{i}=3t$ phenomenon.  Hence for every profile

$$
\min_{O}\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)\le n-\max_{i}f_{i}\le (m-1)t,
$$

and $(m-1)t$ is best possible in the $n$-free uniform sense.  In

$$
u_{\rm uni}^{*}(m,t)=(m-1)t,
$$

i.e. for $m=4$ the uniform $n$-independent guarantee is $u^{*}=3t$.

$$
u_{\rm uni}^{*}=3\times20=60
$$

agents can be forced to prefer an outside item to the chosen set, and

usual $t+1=21\approx20$ first-place, $2(t+1)=42\approx2t=40$ pair form.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The first-place reduction is the whole worst case. 
Write $f_i$ for the number of first place votes, $f_1\ge f_2\ge f_3\ge f_4$,
$\sum f_i=n$ and for $O\ne\varnothing$

$p_O(i)=|\{v:i={\rm top}_O(v)\}|$, $c_j(O)=|\{v:j\succ_v k\;\forall k\in O\}|$,
$j\notin O$.

For $|O|\ge2$ the adversary can keep $p_O(i)=f_i$ on $O$ and can make every
voter whose first choice lies outside $O$ rank that outside item above $O$,
so in the worst case

$\min_{i\in O}p_O(i)=\min_{i\in O}f_i$, 
$\max_{j\notin O}c_j(O)=n-\!\sum_{i\in O}f_i$,

and for a singleton $p_{\{i\}}(i)=n$, $\max_{j\ne i}c_j(\{i\})=n-f_i$.

Put $k=\#\{i:f_i\ge t+1\}$ with $t+1=21$. If $k\ge2$ we can take $O$ to be the
$k$ $t+1$-large items. Then $\min_{i\in O}p_O(i)\ge t+1$ and

$\max_{j\notin O}c_j(O)=\sum_{i>k}f_i\le(4-k)t$,

i.e. $\le2t$ for $k=2$, $\le t$ for $k\ge3$.  The only $n$-free obstruction
is $k\le1$.

If $k\le1$ no $|O|\ge2$ can be made $>t$-loaded in the worst case. The only
worst-case admissible set is a singleton $O_*=\{i_0\}$ with
$f_{i_0}=\max f_i$. Then $p_{O_*}(i_0)=n>t$ and

$\max_{j\ne i_0}c_j(O_*)=n-f_{i_0}=f_2+f_3+f_4\le3t$,

and the bound is tight. The extremal first-place profile is

$f_1=t+1$, $f_2=f_3=f_4=t$, $n=4t+1$,

for $t=20$

$f_1=21$, $f_2=f_3=f_4=20$, $n=81$,

e.g. $21$ voters $1\succ2\succ3\succ4$ and $20$ voters of each of the three
other cyclic first choices. No pair has $\min\{m_{ab},m_{ba}\}\ge t+1$, so no
$|O|\ge2$ is $>t$-loadable. The unique $>t$-admissible set in the worst case
is $O^*=\{1\}$ and the adversary can make

$c_j(O^*)=n-f_1=81-21=60=3t$, $j=2,3,4$,

with $p_{O^*}(1)=81>t$. The balanced $20\!-\!20\!-\!20\!-\!20$ four-cycle
$n=4t=80$ gives the same $n-\max f_i=3t$.

Hence for every profile

$\min_O\max_{j\notin O}c_j(O)\le n-\max_i f_i\le (m-1)t$,

and $(m-1)t$ is best possible uniformly in $n$. For $m=4$

$u_{\rm uni}^{>t}=(m-1)t=3t$,

i.e. $u_{\rm uni}=60$ agents for $t=20$, $61$ on the strict
$\ge t+1$ book-keeping $n-\max f_i\le3(t+1)-1$.  The $21\!-\!20\!-\!20\!-\!20$,
$n=81$, and the $20\!-\!20\!-\!20\!-\!20$, $n=80$, profiles are tight.

The $2t=40$, $2(t+1)=42$, $t+1=21$ numbers that keep appearing are the
same estimate written on the conventional minimal feasible normalisation
$n_0=m(t+1)=84$. On $n_0$ we can take $O_0=[4]\setminus\{j_0\}$ with $j_0$ a
least first-place item, $c_{j_0}(O_0)=f_{j_0}\le n_0/4=t+1$, and
$\min_{|O|=2}\max_{j\notin O}c_j(O)=n_0/2=2(t+1)=42$, i.e. $2t=40$ in the
loose $>t$ wording. That is a normalised, $n$-fixed statement, not the
$n$-free uniform guarantee asked for.

Current consensus in the room is the $n$-free singleton first-place
guarantee $n-\max f_i\le3t$, i.e. $u^*=60$ for $t=20$, $61$ with the
strict $\ge t+1$ accounting, attained on the $21\!-\!20\!-\!20\!-\!20$
extremal profile. The disagreement is exactly the $n$-free $3t$ uniform
bound versus the $n_0=4(t+1)$ normalised $t+1/2(t+1)$ forms. ∎

reflection_text.1:
The first-place reduction is the whole worst case. 
Write $f_i$ for the number of first place votes, $f_1\ge f_2\ge f_3\ge f_4$,
$\sum f_i=n$ and for $O\ne\varnothing$

$p_O(i)=|\{v:i={\rm top}_O(v)\}|$, $c_j(O)=|\{v:j\succ_v k\;\forall k\in O\}|$,
$j\notin O$.

For $|O|\ge2$ the adversary can keep $p_O(i)=f_i$ on $O$ and can make every
voter whose first choice lies outside $O$ rank that outside item above $O$,
so in the worst case

$\min_{i\in O}p_O(i)=\min_{i\in O}f_i$, 
$\max_{j\notin O}c_j(O)=n-\!\sum_{i\in O}f_i$,

and for a singleton $p_{\{i\}}(i)=n$, $\max_{j\ne i}c_j(\{i\})=n-f_i$.

Put $k=\#\{i:f_i\ge t+1\}$ with $t+1=21$. If $k\ge2$ we can take $O$ to be the
$k$ $t+1$-large items. Then $\min_{i\in O}p_O(i)\ge t+1$ and

$\max_{j\notin O}c_j(O)=\sum_{i>k}f_i\le(4-k)t$,

i.e. $\le2t$ for $k=2$, $\le t$ for $k\ge3$.  The only $n$-free obstruction
is $k\le1$.

If $k\le1$ no $|O|\ge2$ can be made $>t$-loaded in the worst case. The only
worst-case admissible set is a singleton $O_*=\{i_0\}$ with
$f_{i_0}=\max f_i$. Then $p_{O_*}(i_0)=n>t$ and

$\max_{j\ne i_0}c_j(O_*)=n-f_{i_0}=f_2+f_3+f_4\le3t$,

and the bound is tight. The extremal first-place profile is

$f_1=t+1$, $f_2=f_3=f_4=t$, $n=4t+1$,

for $t=20$

$f_1=21$, $f_2=f_3=f_4=20$, $n=81$,

e.g. $21$ voters $1\succ2\succ3\succ4$ and $20$ voters of each of the three
other cyclic first choices. No pair has $\min\{m_{ab},m_{ba}\}\ge t+1$, so no
$|O|\ge2$ is $>t$-loadable. The unique $>t$-admissible set in the worst case
is $O^*=\{1\}$ and the adversary can make

$c_j(O^*)=n-f_1=81-21=60=3t$, $j=2,3,4$,

with $p_{O^*}(1)=81>t$. The balanced $20\!-\!20\!-\!20\!-\!20$ four-cycle
$n=4t=80$ gives the same $n-\max f_i=3t$.

Hence for every profile

$\min_O\max_{j\notin O}c_j(O)\le n-\max_i f_i\le (m-1)t$,

and $(m-1)t$ is best possible uniformly in $n$. For $m=4$

$u_{\rm uni}^{>t}=(m-1)t=3t$,

i.e. $u_{\rm uni}=60$ agents for $t=20$, $61$ on the strict
$\ge t+1$ book-keeping $n-\max f_i\le3(t+1)-1$.  The $21\!-\!20\!-\!20\!-\!20$,
$n=81$, and the $20\!-\!20\!-\!20\!-\!20$, $n=80$, profiles are tight.

The $2t=40$, $2(t+1)=42$, $t+1=21$ numbers that keep appearing are the
same estimate written on the conventional minimal feasible normalisation
$n_0=m(t+1)=84$. On $n_0$ we can take $O_0=[4]\setminus\{j_0\}$ with $j_0$ a
least first-place item, $c_{j_0}(O_0)=f_{j_0}\le n_0/4=t+1$, and
$\min_{|O|=2}\max_{j\notin O}c_j(O)=n_0/2=2(t+1)=42$, i.e. $2t=40$ in the
loose $>t$ wording. That is a normalised, $n$-fixed statement, not the
$n$-free uniform guarantee asked for.

Current consensus in the room is the $n$-free singleton first-place
guarantee $n-\max f_i\le3t$, i.e. $u^*=60$ for $t=20$, $61$ with the
strict $\ge t+1$ accounting, attained on the $21\!-\!20\!-\!20\!-\!20$
extremal profile. The disagreement is exactly the $n$-free $3t$ uniform
bound versus the $n_0=4(t+1)$ normalised $t+1/2(t+1)$ forms. ∎
